lessons.title: Calculate vector similarity from first principles
objectives: Represent a document with a fixed-order numeric vector
Compute dot products, norms, and cosine similarity
Handle zero vectors and mismatched dimensions explicitly
Distinguish lexical similarity from semantic truth

sections.heading: A vector needs an agreed meaning
sections.body: A vector is an ordered sequence of numbers. To compare two vectors, each position must represent the same feature in both. Suppose our vocabulary is borrow, tools, hours. The vector [1, 2, 0] means one occurrence of borrow, two of tools, and none of hours. If another vector uses a different vocabulary order, multiplying matching positions produces a meaningless comparison even when the lengths agree. Store or derive the vocabulary consistently. Learned embeddings also represent inputs as vectors, but their dimensions are learned features rather than the transparent word counts used here. This lesson builds intuition with small hand-written vectors; it does not train an embedding model or claim that word counts capture the full meaning of language.

sections.heading: Build the arithmetic step by step
sections.body: The dot product multiplies corresponding entries and adds the products. For [1, 1, 0] and [2, 2, 0], it is one times two plus one times two plus zero times zero, giving four. A vector's Euclidean norm is the square root of the sum of its squared entries. The two norms are the square root of two and the square root of eight. Cosine similarity divides the dot product by the product of those norms, giving one in this example. The vectors point in the same direction even though one has larger magnitude. This normalization reduces the effect of uniformly repeating every word in a document. It does not solve all length or relevance problems, but it makes the comparison more interpretable than an unnormalized count alone.

sections.heading: Define the boundaries of the function
sections.body: Cosine similarity is undefined for a zero vector because its norm is zero. A retrieval application can choose to return a score of zero for that case, meaning no useful directional match, provided the convention is documented. A different mathematical tool might raise an exception instead. Mismatched dimensions should be rejected rather than silently truncated by zip, which ordinarily pairs only as far as the shorter sequence. Validate finite numeric inputs if vectors may come from outside your code. Booleans are a special Python detail: they behave as integer subclasses, so a numeric type check may need to reject them explicitly. Our small function accepts ordinary finite integers and floats, rejects invalid shapes, and uses a documented zero-vector convention. Extremely large magnitudes require additional numerical care beyond this teaching implementation.

sections.heading: Interpret scores cautiously
sections.body: For nonnegative word-count vectors, cosine similarity lies between zero and one in exact arithmetic. General vectors can have negative cosine values. Floating-point calculations may introduce tiny numerical differences, so tests should use a tolerance rather than exact equality for nontrivial decimal results. Most importantly, a large score describes closeness under the chosen representation. The sentences tools allowed and tools not allowed share words despite having different implications. A score does not certify that a source is current, authoritative, or sufficient to support an answer. Inspect the retrieved text, preserve its ID, and evaluate against labeled queries. The arithmetic is a transparent component of retrieval, not a replacement for source selection, permissions, or human judgment about what the passage actually says. Write the feature vocabulary beside your hand calculation and label each coordinate. This simple annotation catches alignment mistakes that a numerical result alone cannot reveal, even when the score looks reasonable.

lessons.title: Audit data quality before indexing
objectives: Validate required fields and unique identifiers
Separate rejected records with actionable reasons
Report coverage instead of only row counts
Preserve a reproducible raw-to-clean transformation

sections.heading: Quality is fitness for a stated use
sections.body: A record can be syntactically valid yet unsuitable for search. A blank text field contributes no evidence. A duplicate identifier makes citations ambiguous. An obsolete policy may be well formatted but wrong for current questions. Separate structural checks from source-quality checks. Structural checks can often be automated: types, required fields, uniqueness, and nonempty values. Source-quality checks may require human judgment about authority, effective dates, permissions, and completeness. Do not describe a dataset as clean merely because a parser accepted it. For the knowledge finder, create a short contract for usable records and a source register for facts that code cannot reliably infer. This keeps the validation program honest about what it can and cannot establish.

sections.heading: Reject visibly instead of silently repairing
sections.body: Automatic repairs should be narrow and documented. Trimming accidental edge spaces in a title is often harmless; inventing a missing ID or policy date is not. When a record fails validation, preserve its row number and a reason in a separate rejection report. The original data should remain unchanged so another person can reproduce the decision. A project can fail fast on the first invalid row or collect several rejections for review. The example chooses the latter and reports one primary reason per rejected row. This is a deliberate interface simplification, not proof that the row has no other problems. If the source owner corrects the data, rerun validation from the raw input rather than manually patching only the accepted collection.

sections.heading: Measure what is represented
sections.body: After checking records, inspect coverage. Count documents by topic, source owner, language, or effective period when those fields are relevant and permitted. A collection with ninety opening-hours notices and one borrowing policy can look large while answering borrowing questions poorly. Track missing categories explicitly. Do not fabricate documents simply to make the counts look balanced. When preparing evaluation data, keep exact and near-duplicate material from leaking across development and final test sets. Repeated passages can make a retrieval benchmark deceptively easy, particularly if the test question was copied directly from the document title. Include realistic paraphrases and no-answer questions. Quality reporting should connect the available collection to the intended user tasks, rather than treating a high accepted-row count as the final objective.

sections.heading: Keep the audit reproducible
sections.body: A useful audit report names the input version, validation rules, accepted count, rejected count, reasons, and known limitations. Save the code that produced it with the project. If cleaning rules change, compare the accepted IDs before and after the change and explain meaningful differences. Stable ordering helps review these comparisons. Retain raw data only for as long as the project legitimately needs it and protect any sensitive content; this course uses fictional records to avoid that issue. Tests should include a valid row, blank text, missing fields, wrong types, and duplicate IDs. Finally, inspect a few accepted records manually. Automation can confirm that a title is a nonempty string, but it cannot establish from that fact alone that the title accurately describes the source or that the source remains current. Reconcile row totals before publishing the audit: accepted plus rejected should equal the number examined under this one-outcome-per-row policy. A mismatch indicates an accounting or reporting defect that deserves investigation.

sections.heading: Assemble a transparent pipeline
sections.body: The final project joins the course's small components. Load fictional documents, validate their fields and IDs, normalize the query and document text, construct term-frequency mappings, score each document, and return the highest-scoring supported candidates. The example keeps documents in memory so you can inspect the entire path; the capstone adds JSON loading and validation from earlier lessons. A Counter acts like a dictionary from a token to its frequency. Sparse mappings avoid creating a large explicit vector containing zeros for every vocabulary word. The dot product sums over query terms, using zero for absent document terms. Norms use all counts in each mapping. This implements cosine similarity for word-count vectors with an implicit shared vocabulary.

sections.heading: Make output behavior predictable
sections.body: A retrieval result should contain the document ID, source text, and score. The ID supports evaluation and citation; the text lets a person inspect the evidence; the score explains ranking only under this particular method. Sort by descending score and then by ID so tied results have a stable order. Keep only positive scores for this simple baseline and return an empty list when there is no term overlap. An empty list means this method found no lexical match, not that the collection logically cannot answer the question. A synonym such as equipment may fail to match tools. State this limitation in the interface instead of turning an empty result into an invented answer. A later semantic method should be compared against this transparent baseline rather than assumed superior.

sections.heading: Evaluate retrieval separately from software correctness
sections.body: Create labeled queries with the IDs of acceptable supporting documents. For a query with one expected source, a hit at two means that source appears among the top two returned results. Average this yes-or-no result over your small query set and report the numerator and denominator. This is a learning exercise, not a statistically strong estimate of future performance. Also inspect queries that should have no match and queries containing paraphrases or negation. Unit tests verify stable sorting, empty-query handling, invalid data rejection, and arithmetic behavior. Labeled retrieval cases check whether the system finds useful evidence. A program can pass all its software tests while performing poorly on meaning, because a correct lexical algorithm still has limitations. Keep both kinds of evidence visible in the project report.

sections.heading: Deliver something another person can run
sections.body: Organize the capstone into source data, reusable functions, tests, and a README. State the supported Python version, the command to run the demo, the command to run tests, and the expected output. List the standard-library imports and explain that no model, API key, external service, or training job is involved. Record where fictional data came from and how IDs are assigned. Include a short failure analysis with at least two realistic queries the baseline handles poorly, then propose a measured next experiment such as adding metadata filters or testing an embedding method on the same evaluation set. Do not claim professional readiness from this single project. The achievement is a reproducible, inspectable foundation that makes later engineering choices easier to evaluate and debug. Ask another learner to follow the README in a fresh folder. Any missing command, assumed filename, or hidden notebook variable is a reproducibility defect worth correcting before adding more sophisticated search features.

example.title: A lexical search baseline
example.code:
import math
import re
from collections import Counter

def counts(text):
    return Counter(re.findall(r"\w+", text.casefold()))

def similarity(a, b):
    dot = sum(value * b.get(term, 0) for term, value in a.items())
    norm_a = math.sqrt(sum(value * value for value in a.values()))
    norm_b = math.sqrt(sum(value * value for value in b.values()))
    return dot / (norm_a * norm_b) if norm_a and norm_b else 0.0

def search(query, documents, k=2):
    if not isinstance(k, int) or isinstance(k, bool) or k < 1:
        raise ValueError("k must be a positive integer")
    query_counts = counts(query)
    ranked = []
    for document in documents:
        score = similarity(query_counts, counts(document["text"]))
        if score > 0:
            ranked.append({"id": document["id"], "text": document["text"], "score": score})
    return sorted(ranked, key=lambda item: (-item["score"], item["id"]))[:k]

documents = [
    {"id": "d1", "text": "Borrow hand tools during sessions"},
    {"id": "d2", "text": "Workshop opens Saturday"},
    {"id": "d3", "text": "Powered tools stay on site"},
]
results = search("borrow tools", documents)
print([(r["id"], round(r["score"], 3)) for r in results])
print(search("astronomy", documents))
example.explanation: Runnable Python 3, standard library only. This retrieves text; it does not generate an answer or use learned embeddings. Capstone work must add the earlier input-validation boundary before calling search.

sections.heading: A prediction is a timed decision
sections.body:
A model starts with a question that can be checked later. Imagine a small parcel service deciding which shipments deserve an additional dispatch review. The prediction unit is one parcel at dispatch. The target is whether delivery occurs after its promised deadline. The decision is whether a dispatcher inspects the shipment. These are different objects: a predicted probability is not the eventual action, and neither is the ground truth. Write all three before touching an algorithm.

Next draw a timeline. Package weight, route distance, and weather observed before dispatch might be available. The eventual delivery scan and a customer complaint submitted afterward are unavailable at decision time. A column can look ordinary while revealing the answer. Ask who created each field, when it became available, and whether historical values were overwritten. This creates a practical data contract rather than a list of convenient columns.

sections.heading: Give each partition a job
sections.body:
Training data teaches model parameters. Validation data helps choose features, algorithms, settings, and decision thresholds. Test data supports a final estimate after those decisions are frozen. A familiar allocation is roughly sixty, twenty, and twenty percent, but no ratio is universally correct. Rare outcomes, short histories, and expensive labels can require different plans. The purpose is independence, not a magic fraction.

Write the split before exploring outcome relationships. General schema checks can inspect every file, but data-dependent choices must respect the experiment boundary. A single look at a test score is not automatically disastrous; repeated changes motivated by that score make it part of development. If that happens, say so and obtain a new untouched evaluation sample when possible. Renaming the same rows does not restore their independence.

sections.heading: Match the split to future use
sections.body:
A random split is useful when records are reasonably exchangeable and the intended future resembles the observed population. It is risky when several rows describe the same underlying person, device, household, or event. A grouped split keeps an entity entirely in one partition. Otherwise, a model may recognize an entity rather than learn a pattern that transfers to new entities.

Temporal splits answer a different question: how well can older records predict later ones? Train on earlier periods and evaluate on later periods without shuffling. Leave a gap when labels mature slowly or feature windows overlap the boundary. Stratification can preserve approximate class proportions in random classification splits, but it does not solve time dependence or repeated entities. Select the split from the deployment question, then report what that split cannot establish.

sections.heading: Make the boundary inspectable
sections.body:
Store row identifiers alongside partition names so another learner can recreate the experiment. Assert that identifier sets do not overlap. For grouped data, also assert that group sets do not overlap. For temporal data, compare maximum training timestamps with minimum evaluation timestamps and inspect the label horizon. A seeded shuffle is convenient for demonstrations, but a seed alone cannot prove that the split is appropriate.

The worked example partitions synthetic parcel identifiers chronologically. It deliberately has no fitted model: methodological decisions come first. Add a short experiment note describing the unit, target, decision time, label delay, permitted fields, split rule, and primary metric. This note should let a reviewer predict what evidence the eventual score will support. A well-defined modest experiment is more valuable than a spectacular number produced by an unclear boundary.

Handle missing and categorical values explicitly
Reuse training statistics on future records
Design feature-availability tests

sections.heading: A feature is a measurement with a contract
sections.body:
Features encode what the model may know. For parcel delays, distance is a measurement, dispatch weekday is a calendar transformation, and route identity is a category. Every feature needs a unit, permitted range, missing-value meaning, and availability time. A distance of 120 could mean kilometers or miles; a model cannot repair that ambiguity. Write a compact data dictionary and reject impossible inputs rather than silently accepting them.

A useful distinction is between fixed and learned transformations. Converting grams to kilograms uses a known constant and does not learn from the dataset. Replacing missing weights with the observed median learns a value. Standardizing distance learns a mean and scale. Selecting the most predictive columns learns from outcomes. These learned operations belong inside the training boundary, including inside each cross-validation fold later in the course.

sections.heading: Missingness has a reason
sections.body:
A missing value is not necessarily zero. Zero distance describes a particular shipment; an unknown distance describes unavailable information. Start by investigating why measurements are absent. A scanner outage, a new partner integration, and an optional field can produce different missingness patterns. A simple baseline replaces numeric gaps with a training median and optionally adds an indicator showing that the original value was absent.

Do not assume an indicator is always harmless or always beneficial. If missingness reflects a historical workflow that disappears after launch, the model may learn an unstable shortcut. Test performance separately on records with and without missing inputs. Keep the same replacement rule for validation and future records. Recomputing a median on a production batch changes the meaning of identical inputs according to their neighbors.

sections.heading: Represent numbers and categories deliberately
sections.body:
Scaling can help methods whose behavior depends on feature magnitudes. Subtracting a training mean and dividing by a training standard deviation expresses a value relative to the training distribution. It does not make the underlying data truly Gaussian. Handle a constant column explicitly because its standard deviation is zero. Some tree-based approaches need little numerical scaling, so use transformations for a reason rather than as decoration.

Categories require a separate plan. Mapping north, south, and west to one, two, and three can imply a numerical order that does not exist. One-hot indicators provide a transparent starting point for small vocabularies. Freeze the training vocabulary and decide how to handle an unseen category. High-cardinality identifiers can create sparse or misleading features; dropping them may be wiser than encoding every value, particularly when the deployment population changes.

sections.heading: Test the transformation like ordinary software
sections.body:
The example learns a replacement value, mean, and scale from four training measurements. A future batch contains a very large value; the learned statistics remain unchanged. That is the property to protect. Keep a fitted transformation object or dictionary and apply it consistently. If a training distribution changes enough to require new statistics, treat that as retraining and evaluation, not an invisible convenience during prediction.

Add tests for missing inputs, constant columns, unexpected categories, invalid units, and empty training data. Also test that transformation does not change row order or detach labels from records. Inspect a few transformed records by hand. A feature pipeline can produce perfectly shaped numeric arrays while encoding the wrong meaning. Your task is to make both the mechanics and the measurement assumptions visible, so subsequent model comparisons are comparisons of genuine predictive approaches.

example.title: Freeze training-only statistics
example.code:
from statistics import median, mean, pstdev
train = [2.0, None, 4.0, 6.0]
fill = median(x for x in train if x is not None)
filled = [fill if x is None else x for x in train]
center = mean(filled)
scale = pstdev(filled) or 1.0

def transform(values):
    return [((fill if x is None else x) - center) / scale for x in values]

before = (fill, center, scale)
print([round(x, 2) for x in transform([None, 100.0])])
assert before == (fill, center, scale)

lessons.title: Understand regression through a small baseline
objectives: Fit a one-feature least-squares regression
Compare against a constant prediction
Interpret residuals and error units
Recognize extrapolation and noncausal coefficients

sections.heading: Predict a quantity before predicting a category
sections.body:
Regression estimates a numeric outcome, such as delivery duration in hours. Begin with the simplest useful benchmark. A constant predictor returns the training mean for every shipment. It ignores features, but it establishes whether a more complicated model adds value. For absolute-error objectives, a training median is another natural constant benchmark. A baseline is a measurement instrument, not an embarrassing model to hide.

A straight-line predictor uses an intercept and a slope. With distance as its input, the intercept is the predicted duration at zero distance and the slope is the change in predicted duration per distance unit. These interpretations depend on the data range and modeling assumptions. If the dataset contains no short trips, the intercept may be a mathematical convenience rather than a plausible duration for a real shipment.

sections.heading: Fit a line by minimizing squared residuals
sections.body:
A residual is the observed outcome minus the prediction. Least squares chooses coefficients that minimize the sum of squared residuals on training records. For a single feature, the slope can be computed by dividing the sum of centered input-output products by the sum of squared centered inputs. The intercept then aligns the predicted and observed training means. If all inputs are equal, the denominator vanishes and a slope cannot be identified from those observations.

The worked example implements this calculation directly so the fitting process remains inspectable. Real libraries provide more robust numerical routines for multiple features and difficult data. Understanding the tiny version helps you ask better questions of the larger one. Squaring residuals emphasizes large errors; that can be appropriate, but extreme mistakes or data-entry problems can dominate the fit.

sections.heading: Score in units a reader understands
sections.body:
Mean absolute error averages the magnitude of prediction mistakes and remains in target units. Root mean squared error also uses target units while emphasizing large mistakes more strongly. Mean squared error uses squared units and is often less intuitive to stakeholders. Choose a primary metric before comparing many candidates. Report the metric for the baseline and candidate on exactly the same evaluation records.

Do not stop at the average. Inspect residuals against distance, predicted duration, and known operating conditions. Consistently underpredicting long journeys may suggest a nonlinear relationship or an omitted feature. A handful of enormous residuals might indicate unusual events, corrupted records, or a genuine model limitation. Investigate with domain context rather than removing inconvenient points merely because the score improves. Evaluation data should reflect the cases the system must handle.

sections.heading: Know what the line cannot tell you
sections.body:
A fitted association is not evidence that changing a feature will cause the predicted outcome change. Distance may correlate with route type, service class, or depot practices. A slope captures patterns in the available sample under the model specification. It does not establish an intervention effect. Likewise, a precise-looking prediction is not a promise that the next parcel will arrive at that exact time.

Extrapolation deserves particular caution. A model trained on journeys between ten and fifty kilometers may generate a number for five hundred kilometers, but that number is weakly supported by its training experience. Record the supported feature range and decide when to flag unusual inputs. Keep the training fit, validation comparison, residual inspection, and deployment decision as separate steps. The final question is whether this predictor improves the actual decision enough to justify its limitations.

example.title: Fit and evaluate a line without dependencies
example.code:
from statistics import mean
from math import sqrt
train = [(10, 2), (20, 3), (30, 5), (40, 6)]
xbar = mean(x for x, y in train)
ybar = mean(y for x, y in train)
denominator = sum((x - xbar) ** 2 for x, y in train)
assert denominator > 0
slope = sum((x - xbar) * (y - ybar) for x, y in train) / denominator
intercept = ybar - slope * xbar

                      ("line", lambda x: intercept + slope * x)]:
    errors = [y - predict(x) for x, y in valid]
    print(name, "MAE", round(mean(abs(e) for e in errors), 3),
          "RMSE", round(sqrt(mean(e * e for e in errors)), 3))

lessons.title: Turn classification scores into decisions
objectives: Distinguish probabilities, rankings, and class labels
Compute logistic scores with a stable sigmoid
Trace how thresholds alter decisions
Explain why calibration and action costs matter

sections.heading: Separate the score from the action
sections.body:
Classification predicts a category, such as late versus on time. Many classifiers first produce a score and then convert it into a class label. A score may support ranking without representing a trustworthy probability. Even an output bounded between zero and one is not automatically calibrated. Keep three questions separate: which parcels rank highest, how reliable are numerical probability estimates, and which parcels should receive an intervention?

A threshold turns scores into a decision. If a parcel is flagged whenever its score is at least 0.4, a score of 0.39 is unflagged and 0.40 is flagged. The boundary is a policy choice informed by evidence and costs. It is not a universal property of classification. A dispatch team with capacity for ten reviews may also need a ranking-based capacity rule.

sections.heading: Read logistic regression as a compact model
sections.body:
Logistic regression combines weighted features into a real-valued number and maps it through a sigmoid. The sigmoid yields a value between zero and one. During actual training, the weights are learned using labeled examples and a classification loss, often with regularization. Despite its name, logistic regression is commonly used for classification. The worked example uses explicitly chosen coefficients to show inference, not a trained or validated model.

A positive coefficient increases the score when that feature increases while other modeled features remain fixed. Scaling affects how coefficients should be compared, and correlated features complicate simplistic interpretations. An intercept shifts the overall tendency to predict the positive class. Check the exact feature order at inference; swapping distance and weight can produce plausible-looking numbers from an entirely incorrect computation.

sections.heading: Choose thresholds with consequences in view
sections.body:
A false positive flags a parcel that would have arrived on time. A false negative misses a parcel that arrives late. For a low-cost review queue, extra false positives may be acceptable if they recover important missed delays. If each flag causes an expensive intervention, the acceptable trade-off changes. Specify estimated costs or capacity constraints before optimizing the threshold on validation data.

Try several candidate thresholds and calculate the resulting confusion matrix for each. Lowering a threshold generally increases the number of positive predictions, often increasing recall while potentially reducing precision. The exact outcome depends on the scores and labels. Freeze the selected threshold before the final test. A threshold tuned on test outcomes can make the final reported performance optimistic even when the underlying model weights never changed.

sections.heading: Treat probability quality as a separate test
sections.body:
Suppose a group of parcels all receive scores near 0.7. A calibrated predictor would have roughly seventy percent positive outcomes across many comparable cases in that group. This is a population-level property, not a statement that any individual parcel is seventy percent late. Calibration can drift when the operating environment or class prevalence changes. It should be evaluated on data independent of model fitting.

For a learning project, start by grouping held-out predictions into broad score bands and comparing average scores with observed positive rates. Small groups have noisy estimates, so report counts. Do not invent confident probabilities from a ranking-only model. A useful classifier report includes the scoring rule, threshold rationale, confusion matrix, and known limitations. That documentation tells the next engineer where numerical modeling ends and operational judgment begins.

lessons.title: Evaluate imbalanced predictions honestly
objectives: Compute confusion-matrix metrics from counts
Explain why accuracy can hide rare-class failure
Compare thresholded and ranking-based evaluation
Inspect slices without overclaiming small samples

sections.heading: Start with the four counts
sections.body:
A binary confusion matrix tracks true positives, false positives, true negatives, and false negatives. Define the positive class explicitly before calculating anything. In our parcel example, positive means late delivery. A true positive is a late parcel that was flagged; a false positive is an on-time parcel that was flagged. Writing these definitions in domain language prevents a surprising number of reversed reports.

Accuracy is the fraction of all predictions that are correct. Precision asks what fraction of flagged parcels are truly late. Recall asks what fraction of late parcels were flagged. The denominators answer different operational questions. Precision describes the usefulness of the review queue, while recall describes coverage of the problem. Always report counts next to rates, especially when the sample is small or the positive class is uncommon.

sections.heading: Rare events expose weak summaries
sections.body:
Suppose only five of one hundred parcels arrive late. A system that predicts on time for every parcel achieves ninety-five percent accuracy while finding none of the delays. That may be unacceptable if the system exists to identify delays. The appropriate benchmark depends on the task, and the majority-class predictor should appear in your comparison rather than being concealed by a polished chart.

F1 combines precision and recall through their harmonic mean, but it does not encode every business cost or use true negatives. Balanced accuracy averages recall across classes and can reveal poor minority-class performance. Neither score makes the decision for you. A metric should answer a stated question. If missing one critical delay costs much more than an extra review, consider explicit expected cost or recall under a review-volume constraint.

sections.heading: Evaluate scores and prevalence carefully
sections.body:
Thresholded metrics evaluate a particular operating rule. Ranking metrics evaluate how scores order cases across thresholds. A precision-recall curve is particularly useful when you need to understand the trade-off between finding positive cases and keeping the alert queue useful. ROC-based summaries answer another ranking question and should not replace analysis of the actual operating region. Different metrics can reasonably prefer different candidates.

Class prevalence affects the meaning of some metrics. A model evaluated on an artificially balanced sample may show precision that does not match a real stream with rare positives. If you rebalance training data, preserve a realistic evaluation distribution and explain any evaluation weighting. Do not oversample before splitting, because duplicate or closely derived examples can cross the boundary. Rebalancing is a training choice whose downstream effects still need independent measurement.

sections.heading: Inspect the places an average can hide
sections.body:
Compute performance by useful operating slices such as route type, missing-feature status, season, or distance band. Choose slices that reflect plausible failure mechanisms rather than searching endlessly for flattering subsets. Each slice needs its record count and positive count. A rate based on two positive examples is unstable; report that uncertainty plainly instead of ranking tiny groups as if their differences were settled.

The worked example calculates counts and precision, recall, and F1 from a fixed list. Its zero-denominator convention returns zero for this teaching exercise, but production reports should distinguish undefined rates when appropriate. Keep the raw counts so the convention is visible. A strong evaluation narrative connects the score to an action, identifies who or what the model misses, and states how much evidence supports that conclusion. Improvement means a better decision, not simply a larger number.

fp = sum(y == 0 and p == 1 for y, p in zip(truth, pred))

recall = tp / (tp + fn) if tp + fn else 0.0

print({"precision": precision, "recall": recall, "f1": f1})

lessons.title: Diagnose overfitting and compare candidates
objectives: Recognize underfitting and overfitting patterns
Use cross-validation without leaking preprocessing
Distinguish model parameters from hyperparameters
Record variability and avoid test-set shopping

sections.heading: Training success is only the first measurement
sections.body:
Overfitting occurs when a model captures sample-specific patterns that do not transfer well to new cases. A highly flexible function can memorize training outcomes, including noise or accidental correlations. Underfitting occurs when the chosen representation or model cannot capture useful structure even in training data. These descriptions concern a model, dataset, and evaluation procedure together; complexity alone does not determine success.

Compare training and validation errors under the same metric. Low training error with substantially worse validation error suggests overfitting, leakage in measurement, or a distribution mismatch worth investigating. High errors on both may suggest insufficient features, an unsuitable model, noisy labels, or an intrinsically difficult problem. A gap is evidence to investigate, not a complete diagnosis. Verify data and evaluation code before reaching for a larger model.

sections.heading: Use repeated partitions to assess stability
sections.body:
Cross-validation rotates which development records are held out. In ordinary k-fold validation, each fold is evaluated once while the remaining folds provide training records. Average scores summarize performance across those partitions; the individual scores reveal variation. Use the same fold definitions for competing candidates so the comparison is not confounded by different evaluation samples.

The split strategy still matters. Grouped folds protect entity boundaries, and time-aware folds preserve chronology. Random folds cannot repair a temporal deployment mismatch. Fit every learned preprocessing operation separately inside each training fold, including imputation, vocabulary construction, feature selection, and resampling. The held-out fold must not contribute those statistics. The final test set remains outside cross-validation when cross-validation is being used for model development and selection.

sections.heading: Tune a small, purposeful search
sections.body:
Model parameters are learned from training records, such as regression coefficients. Hyperparameters define aspects of the learning procedure, such as tree depth, neighbor count, or regularization strength. Hyperparameter tuning uses development evidence to select those settings. Trying hundreds of options on a small validation set can overfit the validation process itself, even when every individual training run is implemented correctly.

Begin with a limited set of hypotheses. For example, compare a constant benchmark with three nearest-neighbor settings and ask whether smoothing improves validation error. Regularization penalizes or constrains complexity, trading training fit for potentially better generalization. It is not a guarantee of improvement. Record every candidate, split, metric, and selection rule. If the comparison supports only a tiny uncertain difference, prefer the simpler or cheaper approach unless other evidence justifies complexity.

sections.heading: Read learning evidence before deciding what to do
sections.body:
A learning curve tracks training and validation performance as training data grows. It can help distinguish situations where additional data may help from situations where representation or label quality needs attention. A validation curve changes one hyperparameter while holding the experiment design fixed. Neither plot supplies a universal diagnosis; contextual evidence remains essential.

The example compares nearest-neighbor regressors on a deliberately small synthetic problem. A one-neighbor model can fit its training records perfectly because each record is its own nearest neighbor. That apparent success says little about unseen inputs. The exercise asks you to record results rather than assume which setting wins. After selection, retrain according to your documented protocol and evaluate the untouched test once. Report both the chosen result and the uncertainty that remains, including sensitivity to data splits and limited sample size.

lessons.title: Package the experiment as a reproducible pipeline
objectives: Separate fit, predict, and evaluate responsibilities
Persist safe inspectable model artifacts
Record data and configuration provenance
Add tests that protect training-serving consistency

sections.heading: A model is more than its coefficients
sections.body:
A usable predictive artifact includes feature definitions, learned transformation statistics, fitted model parameters, and an inference contract. Saving only coefficients while forgetting a category vocabulary or scale produces a different computation at serving time. A pipeline makes this dependency explicit: validate raw input, transform it consistently, calculate scores, and apply a documented decision rule.

For a small course project, plain functions and dictionaries are enough. Define fit(training_rows) to return an artifact and predict(artifact, rows) to return outputs without changing the artifact. Keep evaluate(labels, predictions) separate so target values cannot accidentally enter prediction logic. Larger frameworks provide pipeline abstractions, but the central principle is ordinary software design: every learned dependency is carried forward, and every stage has a clear responsibility and testable interface.

sections.heading: Store enough information to replay the result
sections.body:
Reproducibility requires more than remembering a random seed. Record the dataset version or content hash, row split manifest, feature schema, code version, configuration, and runtime dependency versions where applicable. Record how labels were produced and whether records were filtered. A model trained from a cleaned file cannot be recreated if the cleaning rules exist only in someone’s memory.

Use an inspectable format such as JSON for the simple numeric artifacts in this course. Validate required fields and types when loading. Do not load arbitrary untrusted serialized Python objects, because some serialization formats can execute code during deserialization. A safe format does not make a model valid, but it reduces one avoidable implementation risk. Keep credentials, private records, and unnecessary personal information out of teaching artifacts and logs.

sections.heading: Test invariants, not just one happy path
sections.body:
Unit tests check narrow behaviors: imputation uses the saved value, feature order stays fixed, and the same record produces the same prediction before and after saving. Integration tests check the full path from raw input to output. Add failure tests for missing required fields, invalid types, incompatible schema versions, and nonfinite numeric inputs. Decide whether errors should reject a batch or identify individual invalid rows.

A useful invariant is that prediction must not change fitted statistics. Another is that row identifiers remain attached to the correct outputs. If batches are processed in different sizes, a fixed model should ordinarily produce the same per-record result. These checks catch training-serving inconsistencies that aggregate accuracy metrics cannot explain. Treat performance evaluation and software correctness as complementary layers rather than substitutes for each other.

sections.heading: Design the report as a handoff
sections.body:
The final experiment report should answer what was predicted, when the information was available, how evaluation records were selected, which baseline was used, and why the chosen metric matters. Include the exact model configuration and threshold, not just a friendly algorithm name. Provide a command that recreates the report and state any known nondeterminism or version sensitivity.

The worked example serializes a tiny line model with a schema version and feature name. It demonstrates artifact round-tripping, not production model management. Extend it by validating the artifact before prediction and testing representative inputs. A colleague should be able to inspect the file, run the script, and understand what the result means without contacting its author. This is a practical professional habit: preserve the evidence and assumptions that make the computation trustworthy, not merely the computation itself.

example.title: Round-trip an inspectable model artifact
example.code:
import json
artifact = {"schema_version": 1, "feature": "distance_km",
            "intercept": 0.5, "slope": 0.15,
            "training_range": [10, 40]}
serialized = json.dumps(artifact, sort_keys=True)
loaded = json.loads(serialized)
assert loaded["schema_version"] == 1

def predict(model, row):
    distance = row[model["feature"]]
    return model["intercept"] + model["slope"] * distance

row = {"distance_km": 20}
assert predict(artifact, row) == predict(loaded, row)
print(serialized)
print("prediction_hours", predict(loaded, row))

objectives: Integrate data, modeling, metrics, and operational decisions

sections.heading: Start the capstone with a falsifiable claim
sections.body:
Your capstone asks whether a model improves a dispatch review queue on synthetic parcel data. It does not ask you to demonstrate that machine learning is always useful. Define success before comparing candidates: for example, recover more late parcels than a simple distance rule while staying within a fixed review budget. State which validation metric selects the candidate and which final test evidence will support the conclusion.

Generate a dataset with plausible but explicitly invented relationships among distance, route congestion, missing weight, and late arrival. Include timestamps and stable record identifiers. Avoid making the label a perfectly obvious deterministic copy of one feature, because that hides important uncertainty. Keep a generation seed and document the mechanism so readers understand that the exercise evaluates your workflow rather than forecasting any actual parcel service.

sections.heading: Build the evidence in a controlled sequence
sections.body:
First write the data dictionary, decision-time availability audit, and split manifest. Then implement a majority baseline and a simple rule baseline. Add one candidate whose mechanics you can explain, such as a small nearest-neighbor classifier with training-only preprocessing. Compare candidate settings on development data, select a threshold under the review budget, and freeze the procedure before inspecting test outcomes.

Report the candidate and baselines on identical final records. Include confusion matrices, precision, recall, review volume, and any stated cost calculation. Inspect errors in at least three prespecified slices. If the candidate performs worse, that is a legitimate result. Explain whether the feature representation, data size, operational objective, or model choice should be reconsidered. Do not convert an unfavorable evaluation into a positive story by quietly changing the success criterion.

sections.heading: Write limitations that change behavior
sections.body:
A useful model card identifies intended use, unsupported uses, data provenance, evaluation design, primary results, failure modes, and operational safeguards. Avoid generic language such as the model may be inaccurate without explaining when and what a user should do. For example, distances outside the training range could require a manual review instead of an automatic low-risk label. Missing data rates might trigger investigation if they depart sharply from development conditions.

Monitoring should cover input quality, prediction distributions, review volume, and delayed outcome metrics once labels arrive. A sudden increase in scores is a signal to investigate, not automatic proof of worsening deliveries. Define who reviews alerts and what evidence justifies rollback. Keep an earlier baseline available as a fallback. In this course, the deployment discussion remains a design exercise; no real operations or customers need to be affected.

sections.heading: Earn the next step through demonstrated mastery
sections.body:
Before calling the project complete, run it from a clean directory using the documented command. Confirm that no credentials, network calls, or private data are required. Ask another person, or your own test script, to verify split disjointness, preprocessing isolation, metric arithmetic, and artifact reproducibility. Reconcile every number in the report with a machine-readable output.

The example illustrates a release gate as a set of checks, not a universal approval checklist. A passing gate means the stated learning requirements are met; it does not certify safety or readiness for every production environment. If any check fails, write a focused repair plan and rerun the affected evidence. The professional habit is to make claims proportional to what was tested. Finishing this study prepares you to tackle richer datasets and established libraries while retaining control of the evaluation logic.

prerequisiteBridge.title: Read Python records and transformations
prerequisiteBridge.explanation: A list holds an ordered collection, such as [2, 4, 6]. A dictionary associates names with values, such as {"distance": 20, "late": 1}. A list comprehension applies a rule to each item. A function groups a reusable calculation and return gives its result to the caller. None represents a missing value in these lessons; it is different from numeric zero.

prerequisiteBridge.title: Translate fractions and averages into code
prerequisiteBridge.explanation: An average is a sum divided by a count. A proportion counts cases satisfying a condition and divides by all eligible cases. Multiplying a proportion by 100 expresses a percentage. A denominator of zero needs an explicit rule. Squaring x means x ** 2 in Python, and abs(x) returns its magnitude. These operations underlie the course metrics.

prerequisiteBridge.title: Write a test before a model
prerequisiteBridge.explanation: An assertion checks a condition and raises AssertionError when it is false. It is useful for teaching tests, though production validation should use explicit exceptions because optimized Python may skip assertions. A test should state an expected result independently of the code being tested. A random seed makes a synthetic generation procedure repeatable; it does not make the generated data representative of reality.

objectives: Distinguish model generation from retrieval and application logic
Explain tokens and context budgets without assuming word equivalence
Allocate space for evidence and output
Identify which failures require application-level fixes

sections.heading: Start with the system around the model
sections.body:
An LLM application is a collection of components, not a single clever prompt. A user asks a question, application code checks the request, a retriever selects information, a model or deterministic responder drafts an answer, and validators decide whether that answer can be shown. Logs and evaluation connect the behavior back to evidence. Each component can fail differently, so draw the flow before choosing tools.

Retrieval-augmented generation adds relevant external material to the input used for answering. Retrieval does not update the model’s learned weights. It supplies information for the current request. A document assistant might retrieve a fictional handbook section about equipment returns, then answer from that evidence. If the source is missing or outdated, a fluent model cannot turn it into reliable evidence. The application must handle that absence explicitly.

sections.heading: Tokens are a model-specific representation
sections.body:
A tokenizer converts text into units that the model processes. Tokens may correspond to words, parts of words, punctuation, or other pieces, depending on the tokenizer and language. Counting whitespace-separated words is not an exact token count. Code, unusual identifiers, multilingual text, and repeated symbols can produce very different token-to-word relationships. Use the actual tokenizer or documented service accounting when accuracy matters.

A context window constrains the material a model can consider for a request under its specific interface and limits. Instructions, conversation history, retrieved passages, tool results, and generated output compete for finite capacity in ways that depend on the model. Do not hard-code a model’s advertised limit into a general lesson. Check the current model documentation before integration and preserve a conservative margin for framing and unexpected input growth.

sections.heading: Budget evidence instead of dumping everything
sections.body:
More text is not automatically better evidence. A large bundle of loosely related passages can bury the one sentence needed to answer the question. Select concise, relevant chunks, remove redundant material, and preserve identifiers that let the answer cite its sources. Keep enough surrounding context to interpret qualifiers, dates, exceptions, and units. Truncating a return policy before its exception can reverse its meaning.

Create a budget with separate allowances for instructions, the user question, essential history, evidence, output, and a safety margin. If evidence exceeds the allocation, rank and select it deliberately. Do not silently cut the last characters of a long document and hope the result stays coherent. The worked example uses declared token estimates solely to teach arithmetic; it does not tokenize real text or claim accurate provider usage.

sections.heading: Build an offline first slice
sections.body:
The first version of your course assistant needs no live model. Use a small corpus of invented handbook paragraphs, a basic retriever, and an extractive responder that quotes a relevant sentence with its source identifier. This lets you test data flow, source tracking, budgeting, and abstention before introducing probabilistic generation. Label the responder honestly so users do not confuse a deterministic teaching substitute with a language model.

Write down the boundaries of responsibility. The retriever finds candidates, the answerer uses selected evidence, and application code enforces permissions and output contracts. A better prompt may improve phrasing but cannot repair a broken permission filter. Similarly, a larger context window cannot supply a missing policy update. Learning to locate the failing stage is the foundation for building useful LLM systems without treating every defect as a prompting problem.

example.title: Reserve context capacity before selecting evidence
example.code:
budget = 4000  # Illustrative capacity, not a named model's limit.
reserved = {"instructions": 400, "question": 120, "history": 300,
            "output": 800, "margin": 180}
evidence_budget = budget - sum(reserved.values())
chunks = [("H1", 700), ("H2", 650), ("H3", 900)]
selected = []
used = 0
for chunk_id, estimated_tokens in chunks:
    if used + estimated_tokens <= evidence_budget:
        selected.append(chunk_id)
        used += estimated_tokens
print("evidence_budget", evidence_budget)
print("selected", selected, "used", used)
example.explanation: The arithmetic leaves 2,200 estimated tokens for evidence, admits H1 and H2, and skips H3. A real application requires model-specific token accounting and relevance-aware ordering.

objectives: Design answer and abstention representations
Separate JSON syntax from schema and factual validity

sections.heading: Decide what the application needs to receive
sections.body:
A document assistant may display prose, but the application benefits from a predictable internal response. Define an object containing status, answer, and source_ids. Status can distinguish answered from insufficient_evidence. The answer holds user-facing text, while source_ids identifies the evidence the application supplied. Keep the initial contract small enough that every field has a purpose and a test.

An abstention is a valid product outcome, not a parser failure. If no relevant source exists, the assistant should say that available documents do not support an answer. Do not require an answer-shaped claim in every case, because that pressures the system toward fabrication. A useful contract represents uncertainty directly and allows the interface to ask for clarification or direct the user toward a more appropriate source.

sections.heading: Distinguish three layers of correctness
sections.body:
Syntactic validity means the response is valid JSON. Structural validity means it matches the required fields, types, and allowed values. Semantic validity means it obeys the application’s rules and is supported by evidence. A response can pass the first two layers while inventing a return deadline. Parsing success is therefore only the beginning of validation.

Some model interfaces can constrain output to a supported JSON Schema. This can improve structural reliability, but implementations have supported-schema limits and exceptional outcomes such as refusals or incomplete generations. Check current provider documentation before integration. Even with constrained output, validate application relationships and evidence support. A schema can require a string called answer; it cannot by itself prove that the string accurately interprets the handbook.

sections.heading: Keep validation explicit and bounded
sections.body:
Validate the set of fields, their types, status values, and source identifiers. Reject a source identifier that was not present in the authorized evidence bundle for the request. If status is answered, require at least one source and a nonempty answer. If status is insufficient_evidence, require no fabricated source references. You may still include a plain-language explanation of what evidence is missing.

Decide how errors surface. A malformed response can trigger one bounded repair attempt in a live system, followed by a clear failure state if validation still fails. Retrying indefinitely increases latency and cost without guaranteeing correctness. Never recover from malformed output by evaluating it as code. Treat generated text as untrusted data, and do not let the output choose arbitrary files, database queries, or tool actions simply because it resembles a structured command.

sections.heading: Test the contract before adding a model
sections.body:
The worked example validates a prepared JSON string against a small application contract using Python alone. It intentionally avoids pretending to implement the full JSON Schema standard. You can test the same validator with fixtures: a good answer, an abstention, an unknown source, a missing field, a wrong type, and an unsupported status. These deterministic tests remain valuable after a model is introduced.

Write expected behavior for every fixture and keep failures visible. A model upgrade or prompt edit should not silently change the interface your application relies on. Version the contract when making incompatible changes and explain how older results are handled. The central habit is to design the boundary from the application’s needs, then judge generated content against it. Fluent wording is welcome only after the response satisfies the rules that make it safe and useful to consume.

lessons.title: Prepare a traceable corpus and useful chunks
objectives: Design stable source and chunk metadata
Compare fixed-size and structure-aware chunking
Preserve qualifiers, tables, and document versions
Test extraction and chunk boundaries with answerable questions

sections.heading: Ingestion is where evidence becomes inspectable
sections.body:
Before retrieval, documents must become text and metadata. For this course, create a fictional equipment handbook rather than uploading private records. Give each source a stable document identifier, title, version, effective date, and access label. Preserve its original text separately from extracted or normalized text so you can investigate errors introduced during processing.

Extraction can lose meaning. A table may become a sequence of values without column headers, a scanned page may contain recognition mistakes, and a heading may become detached from its paragraph. Inspect examples from each document type instead of assuming that a successful file read means successful interpretation. If a crucial rule depends on a table relationship, preserve that relationship explicitly in the text representation or use a structure-aware ingestion strategy.

sections.heading: Choose chunks around answerable units
sections.body:
A chunk is a retrievable piece of a document. Small chunks can provide focused evidence, but they may omit the condition that makes a sentence meaningful. Large chunks preserve context but may mix topics and waste the answering budget. There is no universally best size. Choose a starting strategy, then evaluate it against realistic questions and known evidence locations.

Fixed-size chunking is easy to implement and useful for a baseline. Structure-aware chunking follows headings, paragraphs, or other semantic boundaries. Limited overlap can preserve information near boundaries, but it also introduces duplicates and consumes index and context capacity. Preserve section headings and identifiers as metadata. When a procedure has ordered steps, avoid splitting a warning from the step it qualifies merely to meet an arbitrary character count.

sections.heading: Maintain lineage from answer back to source
sections.body:
Every chunk should point to a source document and a location within that document, such as a section title or page range. Track the source version and the extraction or chunking configuration. If the original policy changes, the index must be updated and obsolete chunks handled deliberately. Otherwise, retrieval can return conflicting rules from several versions while the answerer presents one as current.

Stable identifiers simplify citations, evaluation, and debugging. A chunk identifier can combine document ID, version, and a local chunk number. Content hashes help detect changes but should not replace human-readable provenance. Keep authorization metadata alongside the chunk so filtering can happen before evidence reaches the model. A citation that points to an inaccessible source may be unusable to the reader even when the source text was technically retrieved.

sections.heading: Test boundaries with concrete questions
sections.body:
The worked example creates overlapping word windows and records their offsets. It is a transparent teaching baseline, not a tokenizer-aware production chunker. Its offsets refer to whitespace-separated words in the original string. The overlap parameter must be smaller than the window size so the loop advances. Empty input and very short documents should have defined behavior.

Create questions whose answers occur at the beginning, middle, end, and across a proposed boundary. Check whether one or more resulting chunks contain the complete supporting rule, including exceptions. Compare two chunking strategies using the same questions and retrieval method so you can attribute changes appropriately. Keep failed examples rather than discarding them. They teach you whether the corpus preparation preserves the evidence your assistant needs, which is more important than producing an attractive count of indexed chunks.

lessons.title: Compare lexical signals and vector similarity
objectives: Implement a transparent lexical retrieval baseline
Calculate cosine similarity with zero-vector handling
Distinguish toy vectors from learned embeddings
Recognize semantic similarity, relevance, and authority as different properties

sections.heading: Retrieve with visible signals first
sections.body:
Lexical retrieval matches words or terms between a question and candidate text. A tiny baseline can count shared normalized terms. This is easy to inspect: if a question mentions the return window, a passage containing return and window receives overlap. A stronger lexical system can account for term rarity and document length, but start with a method whose ranking you can explain by hand.

Lexical matching has predictable weaknesses. A question about reimbursement might need a passage using refund, and exact overlap may miss that relationship. It can also overvalue common words unless tokenization and weighting address them. Conversely, exact product codes, error identifiers, and unusual names can be highly informative. Keep a lexical baseline even when introducing embeddings, because semantic methods do not necessarily dominate every type of query.

sections.heading: Understand vectors as representations
sections.body:
An embedding maps an input into a numeric vector. Learned text embeddings are designed so some kinds of related texts occupy nearby regions according to the training objective. This does not mean that every nearby passage answers the user’s question, is up to date, or is authoritative. Representation similarity is one signal in a larger retrieval decision.

Queries and documents must use compatible representations. Mixing embeddings from unrelated model versions or different preprocessing schemes can make similarity scores meaningless. Record the embedding model and configuration with the index, and plan reindexing when they change. The course example uses small hand-designed vectors so arithmetic is transparent. It is not a neural embedding model and should not be presented as evidence of semantic understanding.

sections.heading: Compute cosine similarity carefully
sections.body:
Cosine similarity compares vector direction by dividing the dot product by the product of vector lengths. When both vectors are nonzero, the result lies between negative one and one in exact arithmetic. For nonnegative toy vectors, the scores fall between zero and one. A zero vector has no direction, so define a handling rule rather than dividing by zero.

If vectors are already normalized to unit length, the dot product equals cosine similarity. Different indexes and models may use other distance or similarity conventions, and some return distances where smaller is better. Check the meaning before sorting. A high score has no universal probability interpretation. A score of 0.8 does not automatically mean an eighty-percent chance of relevance, truth, or answerability. Calibrate decisions using labeled queries from the intended application.

sections.heading: Evaluate retrieval as a component
sections.body:
Build a small query set with known relevant chunk identifiers. Include exact-term questions, paraphrases, ambiguous questions, and questions whose answers are absent. Compare the lexical baseline and toy vector ranking on this fixed set. Inspect disagreements to learn which signal fails and why. Do not invent vectors that conveniently make every expected answer win and then report that as a meaningful benchmark.

The worked example compares a query vector with three candidate vectors and a zero vector. It isolates similarity mechanics. In the capstone, you can retain lexical retrieval and describe how a real embedding integration would replace the toy representation after separate setup and evaluation. No API call or credential is required to understand the interface. The goal is to keep the representation, ranking rule, evidence quality, and eventual answer as distinct things you can test.

example.title: Calculate cosine similarity safely
example.code:
from math import sqrt

def cosine(a, b):
    if len(a) != len(b):
        raise ValueError("Vector dimensions differ")
    numerator = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    denominator = sqrt(sum(x*x for x in a) * sum(y*y for y in b))
    return numerator / denominator if denominator else 0.0

query = [1.0, 1.0, 0.0]
candidates = {"returns": [1.0, 0.8, 0.0], "charging": [0.0, 0.0, 1.0],
              "mixed": [1.0, 1.0, 1.0], "empty": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]}
ranked = sorted(((name, cosine(query, vector)) for name, vector in candidates.items()),
                key=lambda item: (-item[1], item[0]))
print([(name, round(score, 3)) for name, score in ranked])
example.explanation: The hand-designed returns vector ranks first, followed by mixed. Charging and empty receive zero under the explicit zero-vector convention. These numbers are illustrative similarities, not probabilities.

lessons.title: Retrieve, filter, fuse, and rerank
objectives: Separate candidate retrieval from final evidence selection
Apply permission and version filters at the correct boundary
Implement reciprocal rank fusion
Measure diversity and relevance under a context budget

sections.heading: Use a two-stage retrieval mindset
sections.body:
A retriever quickly produces plausible candidates from a corpus. A reranker spends more effort comparing a smaller candidate set with the question. This division can improve efficiency when expensive relevance checks cannot be applied to every document. In a small offline project, both stages can be simple Python functions, but keep their responsibilities separate so you can replace one without rewriting the other.

The candidate stage should favor useful coverage without overwhelming later processing. If the relevant chunk never enters the candidate set, the reranker cannot recover it. The reranking stage should improve ordering among candidates, not fabricate missing evidence. Measure candidate recall and final relevance separately. This distinction explains why a beautifully ordered list can still fail: it may be ranking only the wrong material.

sections.heading: Filter before evidence crosses the boundary
sections.body:
Permissions, source versions, language, and document type can constrain which chunks are eligible. Apply authorization using trusted application metadata and the authenticated user’s access, not a sentence inside a document claiming that it is public. Where possible, filter during retrieval. At minimum, ensure unauthorized text never enters the model context, answer cache, or user-visible output.

Filtering only after selecting a small top-k list can reduce useful recall because disallowed results may occupy most candidate slots. Search systems differ in how they support filtering, so test the actual behavior. Version filters deserve equal attention: an obsolete handbook can match a question perfectly while giving the wrong current rule. Keep filtering decisions traceable in diagnostic logs without exposing protected text or sensitive access details to unauthorized readers.

sections.heading: Combine rankings without pretending scores match
sections.body:
A lexical retriever and a vector retriever can return scores on different scales. Adding raw scores assumes a comparability that may not exist. Reciprocal rank fusion offers a simple alternative: each result contributes an amount based on its rank within each list, using one divided by a constant plus rank. Contributions are summed for repeated document identifiers.

The constant controls how sharply the method distinguishes early ranks; choose and evaluate it rather than treating a particular value as universal. Rank fusion discards some score information, so it is a trade-off rather than a guaranteed improvement. The example combines two invented rankings with a constant of sixty and deterministic tie-breaking. It demonstrates the arithmetic without claiming that the resulting order is optimal for your corpus.

sections.heading: Select a compact evidence bundle
sections.body:
After ranking, remove exact duplicates and consider whether several near-identical chunks crowd out complementary evidence. A question about eligibility and deadlines may need two different sections. Diversity can help, but do not sacrifice the only directly relevant passage simply to include more topics. Preserve the most useful evidence within the context budget and keep all source identifiers intact.

Evaluate using labeled queries that include exact identifiers, paraphrases, multi-part questions, obsolete versions, and permission boundaries. Compare retrieval-only, fused, and reranked outputs on the same cases. Record latency or operation counts alongside quality when efficiency matters. In the capstone, a transparent rule-based reranker is acceptable if it is labeled as such. The skill being developed is controlled component comparison: know what candidates existed, what filters applied, why the final order changed, and whether those changes improved answers.

lessons.title: Ground claims and make citations verifiable
objectives: Distinguish source presence from claim support
Build claim-level citations using provided identifiers
Handle conflicting, absent, and partial evidence
Implement a deterministic extractive answer path

sections.heading: Grounding is a relationship between claim and evidence
sections.body:
An answer is grounded when its factual claims are supported by the evidence available for the task. Simply placing documents in context does not establish that relationship. A model can ignore a qualifier, merge incompatible rules, or add plausible details that no source contains. Evaluate what the answer says against what the cited passage actually supports.

Consider a fictional handbook stating that unopened accessories may be returned within fourteen days. An answer saying all equipment can be returned within fourteen days expands the rule beyond its evidence. The source identifier may be perfectly valid while the claim is unsupported. Preserve scope, conditions, dates, units, and exceptions. Shorter answers are often easier to verify because each additional factual clause creates another support obligation.

sections.heading: Citations need stable, authorized referents
sections.body:
A citation should resolve to a known source and useful location. Give the answerer an explicit mapping from source identifiers to the selected chunks, and require it to use only those identifiers. Application code should check membership and render links from trusted metadata. Do not let generated text invent arbitrary citation URLs or silently substitute a different source with a similar title.

Citation validity and citation support are separate checks. Validity asks whether the identifier exists in the evidence bundle. Support asks whether the cited content justifies the attached claim. Coverage asks whether all material claims have appropriate evidence. A response can have one correct citation and still include several unsupported sentences. These distinctions make evaluation more informative than a single checkbox labeled has citations.

sections.heading: Represent uncertainty without hiding useful evidence
sections.body:
When sources do not contain an answer, abstain clearly. When they support only part of a multi-part question, answer the supported part and identify what remains unresolved. If documents conflict, inspect their versions, effective dates, and scope before selecting one. If no justified resolution exists, describe the conflict rather than choosing whichever passage appeared first.

Do not treat retrieval scores as proof of answerability. A highly similar paragraph can discuss a policy without specifying the requested deadline. Conversely, a low-scoring exact identifier match might contain the crucial sentence. Your answer policy should rely on evidence content, not only rank. For consequential topics, a document assistant may need additional review and stronger domain-specific controls beyond the course’s fictional handbook setting.

sections.heading: Use extraction as a trustworthy teaching baseline
sections.body:
The worked example chooses a stored sentence only when a simple keyword trigger matches and returns its source identifier. This is an extractive teaching responder, not a language model. It cannot handle broad paraphrases or synthesize complex answers, but it makes unsupported additions easier to spot. A generated responder should be compared with this baseline rather than assumed superior because it sounds more natural.

Build fixtures for a supported request, an unsupported request, a conditional rule, conflicting versions, and a question requiring two sources. For each, write the expected claims and permissible source identifiers. Check both answer completeness and restraint. The goal is not to produce a citation-shaped decoration. It is to give the reader a practical route from each important statement back to the evidence and to make missing support visible instead of smoothing it over with confident prose.
