Keep identifiers in diagnostic output so failures can be traced back without printing sensitive inputs.

For guided practice, change the account-access prediction to escalate and predict both metrics before running again. Then independently design two additional slices and one deliberately ambiguous case. Write a one-page evaluation contract that names the owner of each criterion, the held-out boundary, and the evidence needed to update labels. Your mastery gate is explaining a blocked release using concrete failing cases, rather than arguing that the average looks impressive. Preserve the original failure as a regression example.

example.title: A good average with a failed critical slice
example.code:
cases = [
    ("routine", "answer", "answer"),
    ("routine", "answer", "answer"),
    ("access", "escalate", "answer"),
    ("access", "escalate", "escalate"),
]
correct = sum(expected == actual for _, expected, actual in cases)
accuracy = correct / len(cases)
missed = sum(group == "access" and actual != expected for group, expected, actual in cases)
release = accuracy >= 0.75 and missed == 0
print(f"accuracy: {accuracy:.2f}")
print(f"access misses: {missed}")
print(f"release: {release}")
example.explanation: This fixture evaluates pre-recorded predictions. It does not estimate a real model’s quality or call a provider. The intentionally failing gate demonstrates why aggregate accuracy alone is inadequate.
walkthrough: Line 1: Create a fixed set of synthetic routing observations.
Line 2: The first routine case is correct.
Line 3: The second routine case is also correct.
Line 4: This access case misses a required escalation.
Line 5: The final access case is correct.
Line 6: Finish the four-case fixture.
Line 7: Count correct decisions; True contributes one to the sum.
Line 8: Convert the count into a fraction.
Line 9: Count errors only in the consequential access slice.
Line 10: Require both the aggregate and critical-slice criteria.
Line 11: Print the aggregate to two decimal places.
Line 12: Expose the critical failure rather than hiding it.
Line 13: Print the release decision.

pitfalls: Treating a small synthetic set as representative of all real users
Changing acceptance thresholds after seeing a disappointing result
Confusing grader agreement with correctness
Leaking held-out answers into prompts or development examples

task.title: Build a routing evaluation contract
task.brief: Guided: fix the one access miss and capture the changed output. Independent: deliver eval_contract.txt, a 12-case synthetic fixture with at least three slices, and an executable evaluator that reports counts and blocks at least one intentionally bad candidate. Separate four held-out cases from development examples. Include a paragraph on label ambiguity and sample-size limitations.
rubric: The contract states user outcomes, slice definitions, error consequences, fixed gates, and held-out handling
The evaluator reports numerators and denominators and demonstrably blocks a candidate that passes its average gate but fails a critical slice
The submission includes a corrected run, a retained regression failure, and an honest explanation of what 12 synthetic cases cannot establish

quiz.question: A candidate passes overall accuracy but misses a required account-access escalation. What should the predefined gate do?
choices: Block the release because the critical-slice criterion failed
Release because most cases passed
Remove the access case as an outlier
Lower the threshold after inspecting the result
quiz.explanation: A conjunctive gate requires every mandatory criterion. Overall accuracy does not override a separately specified critical constraint.

quiz.question: You repeatedly tune a prompt after inspecting held-out answers. What has changed?
choices: The set becomes more independent
The inspected set now functions as development evidence
The answers no longer require labels
The evaluation automatically covers production traffic
quiz.explanation: Repeated adaptation to a set compromises its role as independent evidence. Preserve it for regression testing and establish fresh held-out evidence.

quiz.question: Which report best supports interpreting a 75 percent accuracy score?
choices: Only a rounded percentage
Only the best successful example
Correct and total counts, slice results, and dataset limitations
Only the longest generated answer
quiz.explanation: Counts, slices, and limitations expose the strength and boundaries of the evidence.

lessons.title: Trace decisions without collecting secrets
objectives: Model a workflow as related spans rather than disconnected log lines
Separate user-visible latency from accumulated component work
Choose low-risk structured attributes for diagnosis
Recognize sampling and missing-span blind spots

sections.heading: Make a failure reconstructable
sections.body:
An evaluation tells you that a workflow failed. Observability helps you determine where, under which configuration, and with what dependency behavior. For our support assistant, a useful trace connects request admission, retrieval, routing, and response preparation. A trace identifier groups one journey; a span identifier identifies one operation; a parent identifier records its relationship to the surrounding work. These identifiers are correlation tools, not authentication credentials.

Bridge from the previous lesson by giving each evaluation case a stable case identifier and attaching a separate run identifier when it executes. Reusing a case identifier across experiments is useful; reusing a run identifier across unrelated requests is confusing. Decide what question each field answers before recording it. An event named fallback_selected may explain a degraded answer better than hundreds of raw token records. The goal is a coherent account of meaningful operations, not maximum collection.

sections.heading: Read time correctly
sections.body:
A parent duration measures elapsed time across its boundary. Child durations measure work inside particular operations. If two children overlap, their durations can sum to more than their parent’s elapsed time. The worked example deliberately has this shape. Adding child durations and calling the result response latency would be incorrect. Conversely, gaps between children might represent queueing, application overhead, or missing instrumentation. A trace picture alone does not prove which explanation is right.

Use a monotonic clock for elapsed durations in an actual process, and keep wall-clock timestamps for cross-system chronology. Clock differences can distort apparent ordering across machines. Distinguish waiting for admission from service execution and distinguish an attempted dependency call from the result ultimately shown to the user. Record attempts separately when retries occur, while preserving their common parent operation. This structure makes a slow successful request visibly different from a quick initial error followed by recovery.

sections.heading: Design a deliberate telemetry contract
sections.body:
Our example admits only operation and status attributes from a synthetic input dictionary. An allowlist is easier to audit than trying to anticipate every forbidden field. The raw prompt is intentionally excluded. In a real system, even seemingly harmless fields may contain personal information; an operation name should come from a controlled vocabulary, not arbitrary user text. Never assume that hashing a personal identifier automatically makes it anonymous. Retention, access, export destinations, and deletion behavior belong in the telemetry design.

Keep metrics for broad trends, traces for connected execution paths, and carefully scoped logs for events that need detail. Avoid unbounded labels such as every prompt, request identifier, or document title in aggregate metrics. High-cardinality dimensions can make storage and querying expensive. Sampling can reduce volume, but sampled traces cannot automatically support exact population counts. Maintain unsampled aggregate counters for important rates, and describe which failures your sampling strategy might omit.

sections.heading: Practice diagnosis before adding more fields
sections.body:
Save and run lesson_02.py. The parent takes 250 milliseconds while children total 280 milliseconds; no contradiction exists because their intervals overlap. Check that the forbidden field is absent from the exported attributes. If your output says otherwise, inspect where filtering happens. Filtering after an exporter has already received raw data is too late. Apply policy at the collection boundary, and test nested structures if your schema permits them.

Guided practice adds one retry span with a unique identifier and the same operation parent. Independent practice creates two traces: one slow because of queueing and one slow because of a retry. Deliver a short diagnosis that cites span identifiers and explicitly distinguishes observations from hypotheses. Include a missing-parent test and a redaction test. Your mastery gate is reconstructing what the user experienced using minimal safe evidence. Adding a dashboard without demonstrating that reconstruction does not complete this lesson.

example.title: Overlapping spans and an attribute allowlist
example.explanation: These dictionaries teach trace relationships; they are not an OpenTelemetry exporter. All timestamps are invented offsets and nothing is transmitted.
example.expectedOutput:
root elapsed: 250 ms
child work: 280 ms
prompt exported: False
walkthrough: Line 1: Start an in-memory trace fixture with synthetic times.
Line 2: The root operation lasts 250 milliseconds.
Line 3: Retrieval occupies the first 100 milliseconds.
Line 4: Policy work overlaps retrieval and lasts 180 milliseconds.
Line 5: Finish the span fixture.
Line 6: Make a synthetic field that must not be exported.
Line 7: Define the telemetry attribute allowlist.
Line 8: Filter before data reaches any exporter.
Line 9: Compute elapsed time from the parent boundaries.
Line 10: Compute accumulated child work, not response latency.
Line 11: Display the user-journey boundary duration.
Line 12: Display the larger sum caused by overlap.
Line 13: Print whether the forbidden prompt field survived the allowlist; it did not.

pitfalls: Summing overlapping child durations as if they were end-to-end latency
Logging raw prompts first and trying to redact them after export
Using sampled traces as exact counts of all failures
Treating missing instrumentation as proof that no work occurred

task.title: Produce two diagnosable private traces
task.brief: Guided: add a retry span and retain the root elapsed-time calculation. Independent: deliver traces.json containing a queue-delay scenario and a retry-delay scenario, a small validator for parent identifiers and nonnegative durations, and diagnosis.txt. Export only your documented attribute allowlist and include a synthetic forbidden-field test.
rubric: Both scenarios have coherent identifiers, relationships, and timelines, and the diagnosis distinguishes elapsed time from accumulated work
A runnable validator catches a missing parent and a negative duration without printing raw input content
The telemetry contract lists allowed fields, retention and access assumptions, and at least one sampling limitation

quiz.question: Two child spans run concurrently. What can their summed duration exceed?
choices: The number of trace identifiers only
Nothing, because spans cannot overlap
The length of every individual child only
The parent’s elapsed duration
quiz.explanation: Concurrent work can accumulate more component time than the elapsed user journey; use the parent boundary for that journey.

quiz.question: Where should sensitive-field filtering occur?
choices: Before telemetry is exported
Only after a dashboard is created
Only after someone reports a leak
Inside the user’s browser history
quiz.explanation: Filtering must precede the transmission or storage boundary it is intended to protect.

quiz.question: What does an absent span prove?
choices: The operation never happened
Only that the available trace does not show that span
The request was successful
The dependency was fast
quiz.explanation: Sampling, exporter failures, and missing instrumentation can all produce absent spans; absence is limited evidence.

lessons.title: Bound work with budgets and deadlines
objectives: Allocate an end-to-end deadline across workflow stages
Distinguish cost estimates, reservations, and recorded consumption
Select a safe fallback when resources are exhausted
Explain why timeouts alone do not cancel downstream work

sections.heading: Turn a promise into explicit limits
sections.body:
An assistant that eventually answers correctly can still fail its user if it waits too long, spends too much, or consumes the capacity needed by everyone else. Reliability therefore includes limits on time and work. Begin with an end-to-end deadline attached to a request, then track remaining time as it passes through retrieval, drafting, and validation. Giving every stage the entire original timeout can multiply total waiting and violate the user’s promise.

Bridge from traces by identifying exactly where the request starts and where a usable result ends. Decide whether queueing, retries, and fallback preparation are inside that interval. In this course they are. Use integer milliseconds for the simulation and a monotonic clock in a live implementation. Do not confuse a wall-clock deadline representation with the elapsed-time clock used inside a process. Document the conversion and the trust boundary when a deadline crosses machines.

sections.heading: Reserve before starting, reconcile afterward
sections.body:
Time and cost are different constraints. A cheap operation can be too slow, and a fast operation can be too expensive. The worked example uses fictional cost units, not prices or money. Before admitting a stage, it checks whether its estimated duration and units fit the remaining allowances. Accepted stages consume those exact simulated amounts. The third stage is refused because it exceeds both limits, leaving capacity unused rather than violating the contract.

Real estimates are uncertain. Reserve a conservative allowance before dispatch, record actual consumption afterward, and release unused reservations. If parallel branches can spend simultaneously, the reservation update must be coordinated; reading the same remaining balance in two workers is not sufficient. Enforce provider-side or infrastructure limits where available, but do not assume billing alerts are synchronous hard stops. Distinguish a request budget, a tenant quota, and a service-wide capacity limit. They protect different interests and require different accounting.

sections.heading: Make degraded behavior useful and honest
sections.body:
A fallback must preserve the product’s important guarantees. For the support assistant, a short response saying that account-access questions need human review can be safer than skipping a required check to meet a latency target. Label degraded output where that affects the user’s understanding. Never claim a verification step succeeded when the system actually omitted it. Consider reserving time for the fallback itself instead of spending every millisecond on the preferred path.

Bound queue length, concurrent requests, total attempts, and output size as well as individual calls. Overload can produce a feedback loop in which slow requests invite retries and retries add load. Admission control should reject or defer work early enough to protect requests already in progress. Fairness also matters: one large request should not automatically consume the capacity for all small requests. Design the response for an exhausted budget before load arrives, and test it under intentionally constrained conditions.

sections.heading: Understand what the simulation leaves out
sections.body:
Save the script as lesson_03.py and run it. The simulated clock reaches 370 milliseconds and consumes nine units. The refused verification stage consumes neither, because this example performs admission checks before dispatch. It does not demonstrate real cancellation. A client timeout can stop waiting while a remote service continues processing, so cancellation propagation and accounting for uncertain outcomes need separate tests.

For guided practice, reduce the draft estimate until verification fits, then explain which constraint becomes binding first. Independently add a fallback that reserves 40 milliseconds and one unit at admission. Test exact-boundary acceptance, one-unit overflow, zero remaining time, and two competing reservations. If results look impossible, inspect whether you subtracted a reservation twice or compared seconds against milliseconds. Your deliverable should include a budget ledger and a decision table. Mastery means every admitted path has a justified bound, and every refused path produces an intentional result without claiming unfinished work was completed.

example.title: Refuse a stage that cannot fit
example.code:
deadline_ms, limit_units = 500, 12
elapsed_ms, spent_units = 0, 0
steps = [("retrieve", 120, 2), ("draft", 250, 7), ("verify", 180, 4)]
for name, duration, units in steps:
    fits_time = elapsed_ms + duration <= deadline_ms
    fits_cost = spent_units + units <= limit_units
    if not (fits_time and fits_cost):
        print(f"stop {name}: budget or deadline")
        break
    elapsed_ms += duration
    spent_units += units
print(f"elapsed: {elapsed_ms} ms")
print(f"spent: {spent_units} units")
example.explanation: No sleep, request, charge, or external operation occurs. Estimates equal actuals only in this deterministic teaching simulation; a production budget must handle uncertainty and concurrent reservations.
example.expectedOutput:
stop verify: budget or deadline
elapsed: 370 ms
spent: 9 units
walkthrough: Line 1: Set fictional end-to-end limits.
Line 2: Start the simulation with no consumption.
Line 3: Each tuple gives a name, duration, and fictional unit cost.
Line 4: Consider each stage in order.
Line 5: Check the end-to-end time allowance before dispatch.
Line 6: Check the independent work allowance.
Line 7: Reject when either mandatory bound would be exceeded.
Line 8: Record which stage could not be admitted.
Line 9: Do not execute later stages after refusal.
Line 10: Advance the fake clock for admitted work.
Line 11: Record simulated consumption.
Line 12: Report admitted elapsed time.
Line 13: Report fictional consumed units.

pitfalls: Giving each retry a fresh full deadline
Treating a timeout as proof that remote work stopped
Using approximate currency arithmetic with binary floats when exact accounting is required
Skipping a mandatory safety check and presenting the result as fully verified

task.title: Build a bounded fallback ledger
task.brief: Guided: adjust one stage and predict admission before running. Independent: deliver budget_sim.py and budget_cases.json with at least six cases, including exact boundaries and two competing reservations. Reserve 40 milliseconds and one fictional unit for a clear human-review fallback. Produce a ledger showing reservation, consumption, release, and final status for each case.
rubric: Every case stays within the declared end-to-end time and unit limits, including fallback resources
Boundary and competing-reservation tests show that the same remaining allowance cannot be allocated twice
The explanation separates simulated admission from real cancellation and names a safe user-visible fallback

quiz.question: Why should a retry inherit the original request deadline?
choices: To make all attempts take equal time
To eliminate the need for cost accounting
Otherwise repeated attempts can exceed the promised total wait
Because a timeout guarantees rollback
quiz.explanation: The deadline bounds the whole user request, including attempts and waiting between them.

quiz.question: A client times out. Which conclusion is justified?
choices: The remote action definitely never started
All costs were refunded
All downstream work automatically stopped
The client stopped waiting; remote completion may still be uncertain
quiz.explanation: A local timeout does not establish the remote side-effect or cancellation outcome.

quiz.question: Two parallel workers each see five remaining units and each reserve four without coordination. What is the issue?
choices: They can overcommit the shared budget
The estimates necessarily become more accurate
The budget automatically increases
Neither worker can ever finish
quiz.explanation: Reservations need atomic or otherwise coordinated accounting so competing work cannot spend the same capacity.

lessons.title: Retry safely with idempotent operations
objectives: Distinguish transient failure from an uncertain side-effect outcome
Reuse an operation key across attempts without conflating new intent
Detect conflicting payloads for an existing key
Describe durable atomicity and retention requirements absent from an in-memory demo

sections.heading: The dangerous moment after a timeout
sections.body:
Imagine the assistant submits a fictional support ticket. The ticket service saves it, but the reply disappears before the caller receives it. The caller now knows that communication failed; it does not know that ticket creation failed. Retrying as a brand-new operation may create a duplicate. This ambiguity is the central problem of side-effect retries. A read-only lookup and an operation that changes state need different recovery reasoning.

Bridge from the budget lesson by treating retries as part of the original request, with a fixed deadline and attempt budget. Classify errors before choosing a response. A malformed request usually needs correction rather than repetition. An explicit temporary-unavailable response may be retryable under the service contract. An uncertain mutation requires reconciliation or a supported idempotency mechanism. Do not infer safety from an HTTP method name alone; read the specific operation’s documented behavior and scope.

sections.heading: Give one intention a stable identity
sections.body:
An idempotency key identifies one intended operation across repeated attempts. Generate it before the first attempt and preserve it while retrying that same intention. A genuinely new ticket needs a new key, even when its text resembles an earlier ticket. Store a normalized request fingerprint with the key so that accidental reuse with different parameters can be rejected. Include the authenticated account or tenant in the key’s lookup scope; unrelated customers must not collide or learn each other’s results.

The toy service stores an operation result before deliberately losing its first reply. The retry finds the same key and returns the stored receipt, leaving the action count at one. It also rejects the same key with changed text. This captures the API contract, not a complete implementation. In durable services, the side effect and idempotency record must be coordinated atomically or through a recovery design that closes crash windows. A process-local dictionary cannot provide that guarantee.

sections.heading: Bound attempts and reconcile uncertainty
sections.body:
Automatic retries should use an explicit retryable-error set, a maximum number of attempts, remaining-deadline checks, and a delay policy. Randomized delays can help spread load, but do not manufacture idempotency. A retry loop at every layer can multiply attempts unexpectedly, so designate the layer responsible for retrying an operation. Record an operation identifier and attempt number in traces without placing secrets or full payloads into logs.

Idempotency records also need a retention contract. If a record expires before a delayed duplicate arrives, another action may occur. Define the permitted replay window and what the client should do afterward. A timeout followed by an unavailable status lookup may remain unresolved; communicate uncertainty instead of inventing success or failure. For consequential operations, escalating to a human may be the safest bounded outcome. Exactly-once language deserves scrutiny: what is guaranteed, at which boundary, for how long, and under which failures?

sections.heading: Test the crash windows you can explain
sections.body:
Save the worked example as lesson_04.py. The first call records one simulated action and raises a timeout. The second call returns receipt-1. The conflicting third call raises a validation error without adding another action. If your count becomes two, check whether the retry changed its key or whether the code creates an action before consulting its record. If the conflict is missed, check that canonicalization includes every parameter that changes the intended effect.

For guided practice, replay the same call three more times and verify the action count stays one. Independent practice adds tenant scope and a simulated record-expiration policy. Draw a timeline for crashes before the action, between the action and record, and after both are durable but before the reply. State which outcomes your code actually models. Your mastery gate is a clear recovery contract and evidence that duplicates are suppressed in the tested scope, while explicitly acknowledging the concurrency and durability limitations of this small program.

example.title: A lost reply without a duplicate action
example.explanation: The list is a dry-run ledger, not a real ticket system. Recording the action and key in separate Python statements is not crash-safe; durable transactional coordination is a further engineering requirement.
example.expectedOutput:
lost reply; retrying same operation
receipt: receipt-1
simulated actions: 1
conflict: idempotency key reused with different payload
walkthrough: Line 1: Use deterministic JSON encoding for the synthetic payload fingerprint.
Line 2: Maintain process-local records and simulated side effects.
Line 3: Define a toy service, not a network request.
Line 4: Canonicalize this restricted JSON payload.
Line 5: Look for an earlier attempt with the same operation identity.
Line 6: Retrieve the original parameters and result.
Line 7: Detect a key that is being reused for different intent.
Line 8: Reject the conflict before another action occurs.
Line 9: Return the already recorded result for an ordinary replay.
Line 10: Create a deterministic synthetic receipt.
Line 11: Record one simulated side effect.
Line 12: Remember the result; this demo has no concurrency or crash durability.
Line 13: Optionally simulate a lost response after state changed.
Line 14: Make the caller uncertain about the first response.
Line 15: Return normally when the response is available.
Line 16: Start the deliberately failing first attempt.
Line 17: Use one key for one ticket intention.
Line 18: Handle only the expected synthetic timeout.
Line 19: Explain why the next call preserves its key.
Line 20: Replay the same intent without duplicating it.
Line 21: Display the original receipt.
Line 22: Verify there was only one simulated side effect.
Line 23: Exercise conflicting key reuse separately.
Line 24: Change the payload while incorrectly retaining the key.
Line 25: Catch the intentionally rejected conflict.
Line 26: Report the mismatch rather than swallowing it.

pitfalls: Generating a new key for every retry of one intention
Reusing a key for a genuinely new operation
Assuming backoff makes a mutation safe to repeat
Claiming durable exactly-once behavior from an in-memory dictionary

task.title: Specify and test an idempotent ticket contract
task.brief: Guided: replay op-1 three times and show one action. Independent: deliver idempotency_sim.py, at least five tests covering replay, changed payload, new intent, tenant isolation, and expiration, plus recovery_contract.txt. The contract must state key scope, retention, retry bounds, and what happens after an uncertain outcome. Include a crash-window diagram as plain text.
rubric: Replay tests preserve one action and one receipt, while changed parameters are rejected and new intentions remain possible
Tenant scope and expiration behavior are explicitly tested with synthetic data
The contract distinguishes demo behavior from durable atomicity and explains reconciliation when the outcome is still unknown

quiz.question: The first response was lost after a ticket was stored. Which retry identity should represent the same ticket intention?
choices: A newly generated key on every attempt
The original idempotency key
The current wall-clock second alone
No key because a timeout means nothing happened
quiz.explanation: Keeping the original operation identity lets a supporting service recognize and return the prior outcome.

quiz.question: The same key arrives with a different payload. What should the service contract generally do?
choices: Silently create both actions
Overwrite the old receipt with no warning
Reject the parameter conflict
Treat all payloads as interchangeable
quiz.explanation: A mismatch is different intent under an existing identity; rejecting it avoids ambiguous or surprising outcomes.

quiz.question: What is the biggest limitation of the example’s dictionary?
choices: It cannot store strings
It makes every timeout safe automatically
It proves every real API supports idempotency
It does not provide durable atomic behavior across crashes and concurrent workers
quiz.explanation: The demo illustrates semantics; production guarantees require durable coordination and a defined failure model.

lessons.title: Version the whole experiment
objectives: Create a manifest covering code, policy, data, and test fixtures
Use canonical serialization to compare configuration identity
Separate repeatable offline evidence from stochastic live behavior
Build a release comparison with traceable artifacts

sections.heading: Reproduce the conditions, not just a prompt
sections.body:
A prompt is only one component of an AI workflow. Routing policy, retrieval documents, tool schemas, model selection, generation settings, preprocessing, and evaluation labels can all change the result. When a candidate improves, you need to know what changed. When it regresses, you need a recoverable reference state. A release manifest records the identities of the components that jointly define the experiment rather than relying on a memorable release name.

Bridge from idempotency by noticing that identity answers different questions in different places. An operation key identifies one intended action; a manifest digest identifies a specific configuration representation. Neither authorizes execution. Start with an explicit schema and immutable version references for the code, prompt, routing policy, evaluation set, retrieval snapshot, and tool contract. Avoid vague references such as latest in evidence that must support a later comparison. Record unavailable information as unknown instead of pretending it was pinned.

sections.heading: Build a meaningful fingerprint
sections.body:
The example serializes a small manifest with sorted keys and compact separators, then hashes its bytes. Reordering dictionary keys produces the same fingerprint; changing the prompt version produces a different one. This is useful because formatting noise should not look like a meaningful experiment change. Canonicalization is a schema decision: lists retain order, types matter, and omitted defaults may need explicit representation. The simple serializer is appropriate for this restricted fixture, not every possible data format.

A digest detects identity differences under its chosen representation. It does not prove that the code was reviewed, that the author is trusted, that an artifact is safe, or that a claimed external file matches the label in the manifest. Store or resolve the actual versioned artifacts and verify their bytes where required. Protect manifests from unauthorized editing, and avoid putting secrets into them. A secret reference can be recorded without copying the secret value into release evidence.

sections.heading: Separate repeatability from reproducibility claims
sections.body:
The offline examples are deterministic because they use fixed fixtures, no network, and no changing clock. Repeating them should produce identical output. A live generative service can vary even when you record configuration carefully. Therefore reproducibility often means reconstructing the experiment conditions and distribution of outcomes, not guaranteeing identical wording forever. Provider changes, unavailable model versions, retrieval updates, and dependency behavior can limit replay. Record these limits as part of the evidence.

Compare baseline and candidate on the same frozen evaluation cases, with the same scoring contract and comparable run conditions. For stochastic runs, retain per-case observations and repeat enough to examine variability rather than promoting one lucky sample. Change one component at a time when diagnosing a regression, or use a deliberate experiment design when multiple changes are necessary. Keep a changelog explaining why each change was made. A large manifest without a usable comparison is documentation without a decision.

sections.heading: Create a release evidence bundle
sections.body:
Save and run lesson_05.py. The first comparison is true because only dictionary insertion order changed. The second is true because a prompt version changed and therefore the digest changed. If both appear unchanged, inspect whether the changed field was actually included in serialization. If harmless reordering changes the digest, check the sort_keys option and whether your inputs contain order-sensitive lists.

For guided practice, add a routing-policy version and show that changing it changes identity. Independent practice packages a baseline manifest, candidate manifest, synthetic responses, evaluation results, and a small reproduction command. Add an intentionally missing artifact and require your verifier to report it. Your mastery gate is handing the bundle to another learner who can rerun the offline comparison and identify the exact candidate being evaluated. State clearly which parts would remain dependent on a live provider in a real deployment. Completion demonstrates disciplined experiment packaging, not universal control over external systems.

example.title: Configuration order versus meaningful change
example.explanation: The digest identifies the manifest bytes under this canonicalization. Version strings in a manifest do not by themselves verify the content or trustworthiness of external artifacts.
example.expectedOutput:
same after reorder: True
changed after prompt edit: True
candidate prompt: p2
walkthrough: Line 1: Load the standard-library digest implementation.
Line 2: Load the serializer for the restricted manifest schema.
Line 3: Define a stable fingerprint helper for this exercise.
Line 4: Sort object keys, remove spacing variation, and produce UTF-8 bytes.
Line 5: Compute a hexadecimal SHA-256 fingerprint.
Line 6: Name every component in this deliberately small manifest.
Line 7: Represent identical content with different insertion order.
Line 8: Make a candidate with a genuinely changed prompt version.
Line 9: Verify that irrelevant key order does not change identity.
Line 10: Verify that a tracked change produces a different identity.
Line 11: Expose the specific changed component for humans.

pitfalls: Pinning only the prompt while retrieval and tool schemas drift
Treating a digest as proof of approval or authenticity
Overstating deterministic replay guarantees for a live model
Changing both the candidate and evaluation labels without recording the distinction

task.title: Assemble a reproducible evaluation bundle
task.brief: Guided: add policy versioning to the manifest. Independent: deliver a release_bundle folder containing baseline.json, candidate.json, fixture.json, results.json, verify.py, and README.txt. Use at least six manifest fields. Verification must fail on a missing artifact and on an intentionally wrong recorded digest. Document the one command used to reproduce the offline comparison.
rubric: The bundle links baseline and candidate to explicit code, prompt, policy, tool, data, and evaluation identities
Verification detects missing or mismatched artifacts and reproduces the recorded deterministic results
The README distinguishes manifest identity, trusted provenance, approval, and the limits of replaying live stochastic behavior

quiz.question: A manifest hash matches a previously recorded hash. What does that establish under the same encoding?
choices: The represented manifest content matches, not that it is approved or safe
The release passed every evaluation
The author has permission to deploy
The model will always return identical wording
quiz.explanation: A digest is an integrity or identity building block; approval, provenance, and behavior are separate claims.

quiz.question: Why include retrieval and tool-schema versions in release evidence?
choices: They guarantee a lower API price
They can change workflow behavior even when the prompt is unchanged
They make authorization checks unnecessary
They turn random output into a deterministic constant
quiz.explanation: The evaluated system includes its data and tools, so changes to those components can invalidate comparisons.

quiz.question: Which claim is appropriate for a fully fixed offline fixture?
choices: Every future provider response will match it exactly
The fixture proves all production traffic is covered
The supplied deterministic program should reproduce its recorded output
No dependency or configuration record is needed
quiz.explanation: Fixed local inputs and deterministic logic support repeatability of that exercise, not broad claims about live services.

lessons.title: Deploy with enforceable security boundaries
objectives: Draw a trust boundary between model proposals and authorized execution
Apply exact resource and tool allowlists in a dry-run dispatcher
Plan staged deployment, rollback, and permission review
Test malicious external instructions without treating them as authority

sections.heading: A proposal is not a permission grant
sections.body:
The model may propose an action, but a separate trusted component must decide whether that action is allowed. A retrieved article, email, or tool response can contain text that looks like an instruction. It remains content from its original source; it cannot expand the user’s permissions or the application’s authority. This distinction matters even when the text is fluent, urgent, or claims to come from an administrator.

Bridge from versioning by adding the authorization-policy version to the release manifest. A candidate that changes tool access is a materially different system, even if the visible answer style stays the same. Draw the boundaries among the authenticated session, application policy, model output, tool adapter, and downstream service. Mark where untrusted data enters. The support assistant in this course may read approved synthetic articles and prepare suggestions. It has no permission to send messages, change accounts, or access another tenant’s records.

sections.heading: Enforce least authority in ordinary code
sections.body:
The example accepts only the read_article tool and only exact article identifiers from a trusted session allowlist. The proposal can name a tenant, but that field cannot rewrite the trusted session. Unknown tools and unknown resources are denied by default. This small dispatcher demonstrates where enforcement belongs: immediately before execution, using validated arguments and authoritative identity. The model’s explanation of why an action is safe is not the authorization check.

A real adapter also validates types, lengths, enum values, and resource ownership, and uses a downstream credential whose privileges match the intended operation. Keep credentials out of prompts, examples, logs, and source files. Network egress restrictions, sandbox boundaries, and read-only accounts can limit damage if another layer fails. Do not pass arbitrary model text to a shell or interpolate it into a database statement. Parameterization and narrow tool interfaces reduce the space of possible effects. These controls complement, rather than replace, product-specific review.

sections.heading: Treat deployment as a controlled experiment
sections.body:
Before enabling a candidate, establish who can approve it, which environment it enters, and how to disable risky behavior quickly. Separate development fixtures from production data and use synthetic accounts for exercises. A feature flag can reduce exposure if it reliably reaches the execution path that matters; an unused flag is merely decoration. Record the version of permission policy with telemetry so that a denied or allowed action can be investigated later.

Start with offline tests, then an appropriately isolated staging environment, then a bounded rollout if authorized. Define success and stop conditions before exposure. A rollback should restore compatible code and configuration, but it may not undo external side effects or data migrations. Check compatibility and recovery requirements in advance. Security review must also examine observation systems: a well-protected tool can still leak information through verbose logs. Testing should cover both unauthorized actions and unnecessary disclosure of authorized data.

sections.heading: Test boundaries with adversarial fixtures
sections.body:
Save and run lesson_06.py. The authorized article read is allowed, the proposed send operation is denied, and the other tenant’s article is denied. No tool actually runs. The malicious note is intentionally ignored as an authorization source. If the cross-tenant case passes, inspect whether you trusted a tenant value supplied inside the proposal or used an overly broad string-prefix check.

Guided practice adds a second explicitly permitted article and confirms it can be read. Independent practice submits malformed arguments, an unknown tool, a resource outside the allowlist, and an instruction embedded in article text asking for a send. Deliver an attack-test matrix with expected and observed decisions, plus a rollback checklist for the policy change. Your mastery gate is showing that ordinary enforcement code prevents every prohibited dry-run effect in your stated threat model. Passing these fixtures is useful evidence, but it is not a penetration test, compliance assessment, or proof that prompt injection has been solved.

example.title: A dry-run authorization dispatcher
example.explanation: The fixed session stands in for already authenticated server authority. The function is only a dry-run policy check, not a complete identity system, database permission model, or prompt-injection defense.
example.expectedOutput:
proposal 1: allow
proposal 2: deny
proposal 3: deny
walkthrough: Line 1: Represent trusted, server-established session authority.
Line 2: Evaluate proposals without executing any tool.
Line 3: Restrict the tool set to one read-only operation.
Line 4: Deny unknown or effectful tools by default.
Line 5: Read the proposed resource identifier.
Line 6: Reject malformed identifier types before membership checks.
Line 7: Keep malformed requests from reaching the adapter.
Line 8: Authorize using exact trusted resource membership.
Line 9: Create synthetic proposals, including adversarial ones.
Line 10: The ordinary read is authorized.
Line 11: An external-content claim cannot grant send authority.
Line 12: A proposal cannot switch the authenticated tenant.
Line 13: Finish the proposal fixture.
Line 14: Evaluate every proposal without external side effects.
Line 15: Translate the Boolean decision into a clear label.
Line 16: Print the dry-run decision without raw content.

pitfalls: Letting a model-provided tenant or role override trusted session identity
Treating retrieved instructions as permission to expand tool access
Using a broad resource-name prefix instead of verified ownership or exact authority
Assuming rollback reverses actions already taken in another system

task.title: Create a security boundary test pack
task.brief: Guided: permit one additional synthetic article explicitly. Independent: deliver authorization_tests.py, threat_model.txt, and rollback_checklist.txt. Include at least eight cases spanning allowed reads, unknown tools, malformed arguments, cross-tenant identifiers, and instruction-bearing external content. Describe the trusted source of identity and the exact point where execution would be blocked. Do not connect to real services.
rubric: Tests show all intended reads are allowed and every prohibited fixture is denied before any effect can occur
The threat model labels trusted identity, untrusted proposals, external content, and downstream authority separately
The rollback checklist covers policy identity, disable controls, retained audit evidence, and effects that rollback cannot reverse

quiz.question: A retrieved article says an administrator authorized sending a message. What authority does that text provide?
choices: Full administrator authority
Temporary permission until the next request
Permission if the wording is confident
None; external content cannot grant execution permission
quiz.explanation: The authorization decision must rely on trusted identity and policy, not instructions embedded in retrieved material.

quiz.question: Where should the final resource authorization check run?
choices: In trusted enforcement code immediately before execution
Only in the model’s system prompt
Only in a post-release report
Only after a tool returns private data
quiz.explanation: Checking at the execution boundary prevents an unauthorized proposal from becoming an effect or disclosure.

quiz.question: Why might rolling back code fail to fully undo an incident?
choices: Rollback always deletes all logs
External side effects and data changes may persist
Old code never uses configuration
A feature flag necessarily restores all accounts
quiz.explanation: Restoring software does not automatically reverse actions already performed elsewhere; recovery must address those separately.

lessons.title: Respond to incidents and verify recovery
objectives: Prioritize user impact and containment during an incident
Separate incident coordination, mitigation, and communication work
Use denominators and sustained evidence to assess recovery
Convert the incident into owned, testable prevention work

sections.heading: Recognize an incident in user terms
sections.body:
An incident is a disruption that deserves coordinated response because it materially affects users or threatens important guarantees. It is not simply a red graph. For the fictional assistant, examples include silently skipping required escalations, sustained inability to answer, or access checks allowing the wrong article. Define impact in terms of affected users, duration, incorrect effects, and available workarounds. A small percentage can still be serious if the consequence is severe.

Bridge from the security lesson by identifying the fastest safe containment control for each failure class. A broken read-only recommendation might tolerate a fallback; an unauthorized mutation path may require immediate disabling. The first objective is reducing harm and restoring acceptable service, not proving a favorite root-cause theory. Preserve enough evidence to investigate while avoiding unnecessary collection of sensitive data. State what is known, what is suspected, and what remains unknown. Clear uncertainty is more useful than premature certainty.

sections.heading: Coordinate without creating competing changes
sections.body:
Assign a coordinator who maintains the incident state and priorities, an operations owner who applies agreed mitigations, and a communication owner who records updates. In a small exercise, one learner can play each role in sequence, but the responsibilities remain distinct. Keep a timeline with timestamps, observations, actions, owners, and outcomes. Record the exact release and policy versions involved. Avoid simultaneous untracked changes that make it impossible to determine which action helped.

Choose reversible mitigations when they can contain the impact: disable the candidate, reduce concurrency, route to a safe fallback, or stop an affected tool. Each action needs an expected effect and a verification step. A restarted process is an action, not evidence of recovery. If a mitigation increases another risk, make the tradeoff explicit. Communication should explain current impact and the next update point without promising a recovery time that the evidence cannot support.

sections.heading: Measure recovery instead of announcing it
sections.body:
The worked example uses equal-size synthetic observation windows. An error rate above ten percent triggers mitigation; two consecutive windows at or below five percent demonstrate the exercise’s recovery rule. These are classroom thresholds, not universal operational targets. The intermediate state is recovering because one healthy window is insufficient under the declared policy. A later unhealthy window must reset the consecutive-health count.

Real recovery checks should examine error rates, traffic volume, latency, critical behavior, and user-visible outcomes. A zero-error window with zero requests establishes almost nothing. A declining average can hide one tenant that remains broken, and a successful health endpoint may miss the failed workflow entirely. Verify both the control-plane change and the data-plane behavior it was meant to improve. Where side effects were uncertain, reconcile their status separately. Recovery of new requests does not prove that previously affected work has been repaired.

sections.heading: Turn learning into accountable prevention
sections.body:
Save and run lesson_07.py. Observe the sequence monitor, mitigating, recovering, recovered. If recovery appears after the first healthy window, inspect the consecutive-window condition. If an unhealthy window does not interrupt recovery, inspect where the counter resets. For guided practice, insert a seven-percent window between the two healthy windows and predict how the state changes.

Independent practice runs a tabletop exercise for a policy regression discovered during a limited rollout. Deliver a timeline, user-impact statement, mitigation record, recovery evidence, and a short blameless review. Separate the triggering change from contributing conditions such as missing slice tests or a slow disable mechanism. Give each follow-up action an owner, an observable completion criterion, and a priority tied to impact. Your mastery gate is a defensible decision that recovery occurred, accompanied by at least one regression test that would catch the demonstrated failure earlier. A polished narrative without evidence or assigned improvements is not enough.

example.title: Require consecutive healthy windows
example.explanation: This is a deterministic state-machine exercise, not a production alerting system. The positive request counts are controlled fixture assumptions; the task adds explicit zero-traffic handling and more realistic recovery evidence.
example.expectedOutput:
window 1: monitor
window 2: mitigating
window 3: recovering
window 4: recovered
walkthrough: Line 1: Each tuple contains synthetic request and error counts.
Line 2: Start without an active incident or recovery streak.
Line 3: Inspect equal-size observation windows in chronological order.
Line 4: Compute a rate from both numerator and denominator.
Line 5: Use the explicit classroom trigger threshold.
Line 6: Declare mitigation and reset any healthy streak.
Line 7: Apply recovery logic only after incident entry.
Line 8: Count consecutive sufficiently healthy windows and reset on a miss.
Line 9: Require two healthy observations before declaring recovery.
Line 10: Expose the progression so the policy can be reviewed.

pitfalls: Declaring recovery because a process restarted successfully
Reporting rates without denominators or traffic context
Changing several components at once without recording the sequence
Writing follow-up actions such as be more careful instead of testable improvements

task.title: Run a policy-regression incident tabletop
task.brief: Guided: insert an unhealthy window during recovery and verify the streak resets. Independent: deliver incident_timeline.txt, incident_sim.py, and review.txt. Add zero-traffic handling, a critical-slice health check, and at least one regression test. Your scenario must distinguish restoration of new requests from reconciliation of previously affected work and assign three concrete prevention actions.
rubric: The timeline identifies impact, roles, actions, observations, and the candidate or policy version without inventing unavailable facts
Recovery requires sustained traffic-bearing evidence and critical-slice health; tests catch an interrupted streak and zero traffic
The review identifies contributing conditions and three owned, verifiable improvements, including a regression test

quiz.question: A deployment was rolled back successfully. What is still required before declaring recovery?
choices: Only a confirmation that the rollback command exited
A new release name
Evidence that affected user workflows meet the recovery criteria
A promise that no incident can recur
quiz.explanation: An operational action is not sufficient proof of restored behavior; check the user-facing outcomes.

quiz.question: A monitoring window contains zero requests and zero errors. What does it establish?
choices: The system handled all users correctly
The error rate is certainly better than every baseline
The incident is permanently resolved
It provides no traffic-based evidence of successful service
quiz.explanation: With no attempted requests, the window cannot demonstrate that the affected workflow succeeds under use.

quiz.question: Which follow-up action is most actionable?
choices: Add an owned regression test for the missed access escalation with a pass criterion
Be more careful next time
Watch everything forever
Avoid documenting uncertainty
quiz.explanation: A named failure, owner, and verifiable completion condition turn a review into concrete prevention work.

lessons.title: Build an evidence-backed release decision
objectives: Integrate evaluation, telemetry, budgets, idempotency, security, and incident readiness
Distinguish absent evidence from a passed check
Apply predefined staged-release gates and stop criteria
Present a bounded release recommendation with explicit residual risks

sections.heading: Integrate the evidence around one product promise
sections.body:
The capstone brings the course together around the synthetic support assistant. It reads permitted articles, routes account-access questions, and prepares a ticket only in a dry-run ledger. The product promise is deliberately narrow: appropriate routing, bounded work, authorized data access, and recoverable behavior when dependencies fail. Write that promise at the top of your release packet. A collection of unrelated green tests is less useful than evidence tied to the actual service contract.

Bridge from incident response by starting with the failure you most need to prevent and the control that would limit its impact. Link each important failure class to an evaluation slice, a trace or metric, a prevention control, and an operational response. For example, missed escalations connect to a critical-slice gate and a fallback that routes to human review. This traceability makes gaps visible before the release review rather than after a real user encounters them.

sections.heading: Use a gate that can honestly say hold
sections.body:
The worked example combines quality, critical misses, latency, authorization tests, idempotency tests, rollback readiness, and a canary error rate. Missing fields cause a hold. A failed canary gate causes a hold even when other evidence looks good. Fixing the supplied synthetic canary observation changes the output to a staged-rollout recommendation. That recommendation is an exercise result, not permission to deploy a real system.

Gate values require provenance. Store which manifest generated the evidence, how cases were sampled, what time window was observed, and who reviewed consequential criteria. A Boolean saying security_ok is a pointer to test evidence, not an adequate security assessment by itself. Test harness errors should produce an inconclusive or blocked result rather than a default pass. Decide which criteria are mandatory and which are advisory before running the candidate. Explain every waiver with scope, owner, expiration, and accepted risk; do not silently delete failing checks.

sections.heading: Plan a staged release with an exit path
sections.body:
A limited rollout exposes a bounded portion of eligible traffic while comparing relevant behavior with a baseline. Define eligibility and assignment so that repeated interactions receive consistent treatment when necessary. Choose observation windows and sample requirements suitable for the expected traffic and consequence of failure. A handful of successful requests is weak evidence for a rare but serious defect. Evaluate latency and error distributions as well as averages, and monitor the critical slices established in lesson one.

Write stop conditions before starting: a prohibited effect, missing telemetry, exceeded resource limits, or an unacceptable deterioration can all require a hold or rollback. Verify the disable mechanism using synthetic fixtures before relying on it. Name the decision owner and the person who can execute containment. Keep rollout and rollback artifacts compatible. Some changes, especially data transformations or external actions, need reconciliation rather than a simple code reversal. This course remains offline, so your rollout is a simulation with a documented real-world approval boundary.

sections.heading: Defend the decision and define the next learning step
sections.body:
Save and run lesson_08.py. The first candidate is held for its canary result. The second passes the classroom gate. Guided practice removes the rollback_ready field and confirms that missing evidence blocks progress. Independent practice assembles a release packet containing all earlier artifacts under one manifest and introduces two defects that different gates detect. Then repair those defects and present the before-and-after evidence.

Your final recommendation must state the evaluated scope, the passing and failing evidence, residual uncertainty, the next allowed stage, and the conditions that would stop it. Another learner should be able to rerun the packet offline and challenge the conclusion. Mastery requires both a justified hold and a justified bounded go, not merely a green final screen. Completion gives you practice in release-readiness reasoning and reproducible simulations. It does not establish comprehensive production expertise or replace domain, security, accessibility, privacy, and operational review for a real application.

example.title: An explicit release gate with a hold path
example.code:
required = {"accuracy", "critical_misses", "p95_ms", "security_ok", "idempotency_ok", "rollback_ready", "canary_error_rate"}
def decide(evidence):
    if not required.issubset(evidence):
        return "HOLD: missing evidence"
    checks = {
        "quality": evidence["accuracy"] >= 0.95,
        "critical": evidence["critical_misses"] == 0,
        "latency": evidence["p95_ms"] <= 500,
        "security": evidence["security_ok"] is True,
        "idempotency": evidence["idempotency_ok"] is True,
        "rollback": evidence["rollback_ready"] is True,
        "canary": evidence["canary_error_rate"] <= 0.02,
    }
    failures = [name for name, passed in checks.items() if not passed]
    return "HOLD: " + ", ".join(failures) if failures else "GO: staged rollout"
candidate = dict(accuracy=0.97, critical_misses=0, p95_ms=450, security_ok=True, idempotency_ok=True, rollback_ready=True, canary_error_rate=0.04)
print(decide(candidate))
candidate["canary_error_rate"] = 0.01
print(decide(candidate))
example.explanation: This teaching gate assumes correctly typed, finite, validated numeric evidence. The independent task adds schema validation, provenance, and sample counts. Updating a fixture is not a substitute for collecting fresh real evidence.

pitfalls: Treating a missing report as a passed criterion
Replacing failed measurements with desired numbers rather than rerunning the experiment
Claiming a tiny canary proves absence of rare failures
Letting a release script imply authorization for a real deployment

task.title: Submit the complete release-readiness packet
task.brief: Guided: remove rollback_ready and demonstrate a hold for missing evidence. Independent: deliver release_packet with README.txt, manifest.json, fixtures.json, evaluation results, private trace examples, budget and idempotency tests, security tests, an incident runbook, and release_gate.py. Validate evidence types, finite numbers, sensible ranges, provenance, and minimum sample counts. Inject at least two different defects, show the hold reasons, repair them through reruns, and present a bounded simulated rollout recommendation. No real deployment or external action is part of this task.
rubric: The packet reruns offline with one documented command and connects every reported result to the same versioned candidate and stated sampling scope
At least two injected defects plus missing or malformed evidence produce appropriate holds, and corrected reruns demonstrate all mandatory gates
The release recommendation includes residual risks, staged exposure, stop and rollback criteria, ownership, and a clear boundary requiring separate real-world approval

quiz.question: A required rollback-readiness report is absent. How should the gate treat it?
choices: Assume rollback is ready
Hold for missing evidence
Ignore the field if accuracy is high
Replace it with the previous candidate’s result without checking compatibility
quiz.explanation: Required evidence must be present and applicable to the candidate; absence cannot count as a passing result.

quiz.question: What turns a limited rollout into a controlled learning step?
choices: Sending all traffic immediately
Waiting until somebody complains
Predefined eligibility, observation requirements, acceptance gates, and stop conditions
Checking only the best response
quiz.explanation: A bounded rollout needs a deliberate comparison and exit policy so evidence can guide exposure.

quiz.question: After fixing a failed implementation, what evidence should replace its failed result?
choices: A manually edited passing number
A confident explanation alone
A screenshot from an unrelated baseline
A fresh run of the relevant versioned tests under the same stated contract
quiz.explanation: Corrected code needs new evidence; editing the outcome would erase the relationship between experiment and decision.
